articles.title: Who is Martin Romualdez?
articles.summary: Born on November 14, 1963, Romualdez is the son of the late Leyte governor and diplomat Benjamin “Kokoy” Romualdez and Juliette Romualdez. He is also known as a “presidential cousin,” being one of…

blocks.text: Published September 7, 2026 11:14pm
Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez has been placed under arrest on plunder charges, allegations that he has repeatedly denied and which his lawyer said he is ready to face in court.
Born on November 14, 1963, Romualdez is the son of the late Leyte governor and diplomat Benjamin “Kokoy” Romualdez and Juliette Romualdez.
He is also known as a “presidential cousin,” being one of the first cousins of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and Senator Imee Marcos.
His father is a brother of former first lady Imelda Marcos, the President’s mother.
Romualdez is married to Tingog Party-list Representative Yedda Marie Romualdez, with whom he has four children.
Romualdez has been the representative of Leyte's 1st congressional district from 2007 until 2016, and from 2019 to the present. His current term will run until 2028.
In July 2022, he was elected Speaker of the House of Representatives in the 19th Congress and was reelected for the 20th Congress with no other lawmaker nominated for the post.
He launched a nationwide campaign for the Senate during the 2016 national elections, ultimately missing a seat after finishing 15th in the final vote tally.

Before entering public service, Romualdez earned a Bachelor of Arts in Government from Cornell University in 1985. He went on to finish his law degree at the University of the Philippines College of Law in 1992 and passed the Philippine Bar Examinations in 1993.
Flood control scandal

On Monday, September 7, the Office of the Ombudsman officially lodged a P7.4-billion plunder case against Romualdez, former House appropriations committee head Zaldy Co (Ako Bicol party-list), Romualdez's personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Serenio, and Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation president Felicito Cristobal Guevarra.

The formal charge alleges that Romualdez and Co leveraged their official positions to routinely collect kickbacks, shares, and other financial gains totaling a minimum of P7.4 billion across at least 15 separate instances.
Later that same day, the Sandiganbayan Third Division issued warrants of arrest against them.

"The issuance of a warrant of arrest signifies only that, after personally evaluating the records, the Court found probable cause to believe that the accused committed the offense charged," the Third Division said.

"Probable cause for the issuance of a warrant of arrest exists when the facts and circumstances alleged by the prosecution would lead a reasonably discreet and prudent person to believe that an offense has been committed by the person sought to be arrested," it added.
Romualdez has been placed under arrest at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, where he is confined, citing cardiovascular health and a brain condition. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: French winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heat
articles.summary:
Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality

French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report…

blocks.text: French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry.
Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.

Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result of extreme weather conditions.

“The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported.

blocks.caption: A grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA

blocks.text: However, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions.

The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported.

A series of heatwaves brought the highest summer temperatures recorded in France since records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C.

Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported.

Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production.
However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards.

“We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.”

blocks.caption: The harvest under way early in the morning at Trois Terres. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA

blocks.text: Some Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? I have absolutely no idea how the ministry has come up with these figures.”
after newsletter promotion

Agreste said the figures were estimates and definitive results would not be known until regions made official harvest declarations later this year. It added that 2026 grape harvests were “marked by significant regional disparities”.

Wine harvests have traditionally taken place in France between September and mid October, but the climate emergency has brought dates forward slightly each year for the last four decades. This year, the harvest timetable advanced at least a week compared with last year throughout the country. Some vineyards in Bordeaux began two weeks early.

There are also concerns that vines and grapes in some of France’s best-known wine producing regions, including Bordeaux, have been damaged by smoke from rampant wildfires. No major Bordeaux vineyards suffered direct damage from the flames that came within 15km (9 miles) of the city, but there is concern that smoke has entered the grape skins causing “smoke taint” and affecting the taste of the finished wine.

The agriculture ministry would normally issue harvest estimates in early August, but postponed its analysis at the request of the wine industry because of what it described as “the high level of uncertainty surrounding these forecasts” caused by weather conditions and wildfires.
France’s wine sector is already under pressure owing to a decline in demand. Annual wine consumption in the 1960s in France was 127 litres each year compared with 40 litres a year now.
Wine drinking in the US, France’s largest export market, has also dropped and French wines have been hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs.

articles.title: War criminal Ratko Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade, Serbia
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb commander convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, has been buried in Belgrade. The funeral, broadcast live on TV, comes just days before President Vucic is expected…

image.caption: Former Bosnian Serb army commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on MondayImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.

Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.

Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.
President Vucic not in attendance
President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.
Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.

blocks.caption: Thousands gathered in the Serbian capital to witness Mladic's funeral procession Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.
"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.
The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.

Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.

An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Politically tricky time for Vucic
For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.
He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.

blocks.caption: Mladic was buried with military honorsImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.
Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.
Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina
According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.

"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."

Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.

blocks.caption: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has brushed aside criticism from the European UnionImage: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.
"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."
Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.
Students have a different focus

In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.

Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.
In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.
The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.

blocks.caption: The student movement, which has been leading anti-government protests in Serbia for almost two years, has largely avoided commenting on Mladic or arrangements for his funeral. Pictured here: people at a protest rally in JuneImage: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW

blocks.text: The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.
Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.
The power of media control
Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.
The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.
In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."

Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.
Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.

articles.title: Stolen Generations survivors have more health challenges than other First Nations people
articles.summary:
Indigenous Australians forcibly removed under government policies more likely to have severe or profound disability, report finds

  • Get our

blocks.text: The tens of thousands of Indigenous Australians and their descendents who were forcibly removed under government assimilation policies have far greater physical and health challenges when compared to the wider Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations, according to a new report.

The report by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) was commissioned by peak advocacy body the Healing Foundation, which supports Stolen Generations survivors and their families, and builds on existing data released in 2023.

Released on Tuesday, the report reveals the stark inequities and the long-term inter-generational impacts of forced removals, a policy adopted by all Australian governments up to the 1970s under racist assimilation laws.

Children were put into institutions, or were fostered or adopted out to non-Indigenous families where many of them suffered harsh, degrading treatment and sexual abuse after being taken from their families. It is estimated at least one in 10 and possibly as many as one in three Indigenous children were removed from their families between 1910 and 1970.
The report uses survey data from 2022 and 2023 of Stolen Generation members, who are now all over the age of 50, and their descendants.
About 200,0000 people – or 45% of Indigenous Australians – have a parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle who was removed from their family, the report said.

Survivors were 2.7 times more likely to have severe or profound disability than other Indigenous Australians, and 1.7 times as likely to have been admitted to hospital in the past 12 months even when differences such as age, sex and remoteness of location were taken into account.

Compared to non-Indigenous Australians, survivors were six times more likely to have kidney disease, 4.8 times more likely to have a severe or profound disability, and 3.9 times more likely to report high psychological distress.

The report also found that Stolen Generations survivors experienced greater socio-economic challenges and distress, such as being less likely to be able to pay for unexpected emergency costs, or experiencing more days where they were unable to afford their essential needs.
after newsletter promotion
“In summary, the collective pattern indicates that Stolen Generations survivors experience generally more challenging socioeconomic circumstances than other Indigenous people,” the report said.

The report also found that Stolen Generations survivors were nearly twice as likely as other Indigenous peoples to report high levels of psychological distress, and 1.6 times likely to report experiencing mental or behavioural health conditions. Their descendants were 1.3 times more likely both to report high psychological distress and to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.
Dr Martin Edvardsson, the acting head of First Nations health at AIHW, said Australia lacked comprehensive data on the experiences and needs of Stolen Generation survivors and their families.

“Understanding the needs of Stolen Generations survivors through the existing data sources will be increasingly challenging as survivors grow older and become less well represented in household surveys,” Edvardsson said.

articles.title: Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
articles.summary: A visibly shaken but also determined Friedrich Merz spoke in Berlin about the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt and the CDU's bitter defeat. He insisted on sticking to his reforms.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Saxony-Anhalt's Premier Sven Schulze spoke about the impact of the electionImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are situations in which politicians who have little left to say to each other still appear together before the press. This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.

He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."

This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.
No regard for the rule of law?
Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.

But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.

In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."
Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.

Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."
What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany
Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?

Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.
As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.

And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?
If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.
Merz defends his controversial reforms

However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.

On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.
How the AfD changed its pitch and broke through
AfD displays confidence

Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.
"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."
For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.

Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."

But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Romualdez asks court to extend hospital confinement after arrest
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Monday asked the Sandiganbayan Third Division to extend his hospital confinement following his arrest for plunder. Currently, Romualdez…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Monday asked the Sandiganbayan Third Division to extend his hospital confinement following his arrest for plunder.
Currently, Romualdez is confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.
Authorities issued Romualdez’s arrest warrant and underwent booking procedures while confined to his bed.
LIVE UPDATES: Ex-Speaker Romualdez faces arrest over plunder raps

In his nine-page Manifestation of Hospital Confinement and Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement under custody Romualdez said he wished to be under continuous lawful custody at the hospital “for so long as inpatient confinement remains medically necessary, certified by his attending physician, until he is medically cleared for transfer.”

“The requested accommodation rests exclusively on documented medical necessity, remains subject to continuous custody and judicial supervision, and may be independently verified by a court-designated or government physician,” Romualdez said.
He said he was confined in the hospital on Monday due to Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism, and other illnesses.

“The required care cannot, at this time, be safely delivered at a detention facility hospital, much less a detention facility, and identifies the clinical milestones or conditions upon which the accused may be medically cleared for transfer,” the motion said.
Dennis Pulma, Sandiganbayan Third Division clerk of court, said the anti-graft court sheriff also went to the hospital to implement the arrest warrant.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only the Court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant,” Pulma said in a text message.
“Until the Court orders otherwise, the warrant remains in force and must be implemented,” he said.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co and two others hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the information containing the formal charges against the accused.

According to the information containing the formal charges filed by prosecutors before the anti-graft court, Romualdez and Co were charged with “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons, and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure, and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, according to the information.
Furthermore, the information stated that this amount was “specifically traced and laundered in setting up and/or using shell or dummy corporations and conduits” allegedly received by Sereño.
According to the Ombudsman’s resolution, Romualdez allegedly gave a P2 billion monthly “quota” for kickbacks.
Romualdez, in response, said he respects the legal process and will face the allegations against him in accordance with the law, according to his counsel Ade Fajardo. /mcm/cb

articles.title: Matibag: Cayetano may face raps over 2019 SEA Games irregularities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Alan Peter Cayetano may be included as a respondent in the charges that the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will recommend to the Department of Justice (DOJ) over…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Alan Peter Cayetano may be included as a respondent in the charges that the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will recommend to the Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged irregularities in the Philippine Southeast Asian Games Organizing Committee (Phisgoc)’s hosting of the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games, according to NBI Director Melvin Matibag.
Matibag said this in an interview on Monday after announcing that the bureau is set to recommend filing cases against five members of the Phisgoc board of trustees, among others, in the coming days.

“He [Cayetano] introduced himself as the chairman. So it’s an ultra vires act. Pinakilala niyang chairman siya na parang nagpapatakbo. So posible na kasama siya,” Matibag said when asked if the senator would also be included in the case recommendation.
(He [Cayetano] introduced himself as the chairman. So it’s an ultra vires act. He introduced himself as the chairman as if he were running (Phisgoc). So it is possible that he will be included.)
The NBI director, meanwhile, did not specify what charges might be recommended against Cayetano and the Phisgoc officials.
According to Matibag, he met with two witnesses this Monday, noting that their testimonies regarding the supposed irregularities involving Phisgoc during the 2019 SEA Games strengthened the case.
He also said the bureau discovered that the P55-million SEA Games cauldron was contracted to different contractors.
“Siguradong may makakasuhan at siguradong may pagkakamali. Nakita na namin, very important ’yung kanina nakausap namin na witness,” said Matibag.
(Someone will definitely be charged, and definitely, there was an irregularity. We have seen it; the witness we spoke to earlier is very important.)
“Mas lalong dumami pa ’yung mga dokumento. I think we will need a few additional days this week para matapos namin,” he also said.
(The documents are piling up. I think we will need a few additional days this week to finish them.)
The Inquirer reached out to Cayetano about the matter but has yet to issue a statement as of press time.

Matibag earlier said that based on their initial findings, Phisgoc received around P6.7 billion in government funds, specifically from the Philippine Sports Commission, the Philippine Olympic Committee, and the Department of Budget and Management for the 2019 SEA Games.
He noted that if adding the other funds Phisgoc accepted from the private sector, the committee’s budget may reach over P10 billion. /cb

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Police arrested 10 people allegedly caught gambling illegally in Barangay Tablac here on Sunday, Sept. 6.
The Candon City Police Station conducted the operation after receiving information about illegal gambling activities in the area.
Police said six of the suspects were caught playing the card game “tong-its” at two separate tables, while four others were apprehended while playing mahjong.
The 10 suspects were taken into police custody and are facing charges related to illegal gambling.
The Candon police said it would continue operations against illegal gambling and urged residents to report information on illicit activities to the nearest police station. /mcm

articles.title: Record strength El Niño could mean bigger supermarket bills for Australians, experts warn
articles.summary:
Predicted hot and dry weather in growing areas in eastern Australia identified as ‘one of the key issues’ that will affect food prices over next 12 months

  • Get our

blocks.text: The most severe El Niño weather event on record threatens to push food prices higher this year, experts say, piling pressure on households already struggling with the post-pandemic spike in grocery bills and complicating the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation back under control.
The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast El Niño will peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.

Michael Harvey, a consumer food analyst at Rabobank research, said the predicted hot and dry weather in key growing areas in eastern Australia was “clearly one of the key issues that will have an impact on food pricing over the next 12 months”.
The Food and Agricultural Organisation in its latest update reported rising weather-related threats are already being reflected in high and climbing global commodity prices.
“It’s a very volatile time, and there are lots of risks around cost re-escalation in the food system. There is absolutely risk of food inflation coming through at the consumer end,” Harvey said.

Not all commodities are heading in the same direction, however. For example, dairy and meat prices are beginning to ease after a big recent rise as the underlying fundamentals in those markets shift independently of the looming weather event.
In Australia El Niño created a risk for what is still expected to be a strong winter wheat crop this year, Harvey said.
“That will be the big thing to watch, as well as the spillover effects of that into things like feed grains,” he said, adding that the ultimate impact would be clear by the final quarter of the year.
Even absent hotter and drier weather, overseas shocks have already pushed commodity price benchmarks higher this year, which are linked to local markets through the export trade.
Dennis Voznesenski, CBA’s agricultural economist, said global wheat prices are up by around a third since the start of July, versus about 9% in Australia.
The extreme weather warnings also come as the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed past US$97 a barrel on Monday afternoon to be 35% higher since the start of July.
With diesel prices on the rise again – a key cost for farmers – fertiliser suppliers have also warned of ongoing supply disruptions that will keep prices structurally higher.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine’s record grain harvests are struggling to find their way to international markets following tit-for-tat attacks on critical Black Sea ports.
“A third of global grain exports are stuck right now,” Voznesenski said.
The past five years have seen rapid increases in prices across a range of supermarket goods, contributing to an entrenched cost-of-living crisis across Australia.
In the five years to June, for example, the cost of staples such as breads and cereals, dairy, and other products, such as jams and eggs, jumped by between 28 and 30%.

In comparison, in the preceding five-year period to mid-2021, the cumulative increase in these supermarket shelf items was 3-6%, according to analysis of quarterly Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

RBA officials are concerned that a particularly severe El Niño could drive food prices higher and create a further headache later this year, at a time when the central bank is already contemplating whether it needs to hike interest rates again.

But Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said it was not easy to show a clear link between El Niño events and higher food prices, saying there were a range of costs – from labour to freight and packaging – that often played a bigger role in determining how much Australians pay at the checkout.
“It won’t be a first-order influence on overall inflation, but if you get a little bit extra from food prices, then it’s unhelpful,” Kearns said.

articles.title: Grassroots Labor group urges Albanese government to chart course away from ‘American war machine’
articles.summary: Pressure follows revelations US military and weapons manufacturers control or have access to more than 100 bases across Australian continent

blocks.text: The US has “led Australia into wars of aggression” for 50 years, internal party campaign group Labor Against War has argued, urging the government to chart a foreign policy independent “from the American war machine”.

The Australian government has defended the growing presence of the US military on the Australian continent, insisting the defence sites “are Australian bases under Australian control”, despite evidence the US military controls more than a dozen bases on Australian territory.
On Monday, the Guardian published data showing the US military, and US weapons manufacturers, control or have access to more than 100 bases across the Australian continent.

The Guardian has detailed 17 military facilities on Australian soil which are controlled by the United States military. The military has access to 75 more Australian-run bases, and US defence corporations access to 18 more.

In total, the US military and American defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia. That analysis has not been contradicted. The data was compiled by Dr Richard Tanter, senior research associate with the US-based Nautilus Institute.
The publication of the database has exposed disquiet within the Labor party over growing US military presence across the continent.

Marcus Strom, the national convener of the grassroots Labor Against War group, said “the latticework of US bases and facilities across our continent should alarm anyone that values Australia’s independence from the American war machine”.
“For more than 50 years the US has led Australia into wars of aggression,” Strom said.
“Labor Against War calls on the Albanese government to chart a new course for Australia’s foreign and defence policy that is suited to the future, not clinging to the fading guarantees of the past.”
Strom said the government should abandon the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement as a first step.
In question time in the Senate, Greens senator David Shoebridge asked the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, why the government had chosen to “sign us up to the next US war”.
Wong said the government would resolutely defend the US alliance, and that “everything the government is doing is working to deter and avert conflict”.
“We are of the view that the US alliance contributes to Australian sovereignty. It enables us to have access to a range of capability that Australia would not have access to,” she said.
Wong told the Senate the US military presence in the country is “at Australia’s invitation”.
“These are Australian bases under Australian command.”
after newsletter promotion

Shoebridge said Australians living near US military facilities in Australia feared they could be targets in the event of conflict in the region, citing attacks on US bases in the Middle East in the current war with Iran.
“These bases obviously make Australia a target when the US decides to start its next forever war, don’t they?”
Shoebridge asked Wong to specify one instance where Australia had said no to the US having access to an Australian military base.
“Access to and use of Australian facilities … is on a rotational basis, mutually determined and at Australia’s invitation,” Wong said.

Pine Gap, the best known of the US-Australia “joint defence facilities” on Australian territory, was established by the CIA in the 1960s near Alice Springs. US National Security Agency documents, leaked by whistleblower Edward Snowden, show the “chief of facility” at Pine Gap is always an American, who reports directly the US National Reconnaissance Office. The deputy is a senior Australian Signals Directorate official.

Former defence minister Christopher Pyne described Pine Gap in a public hearing as “more American than Australian”. There are numerous other bases on the Australian mainland that are controlled by the US rather than Australia, including the GPS monitoring station at RAAF Edinburgh base in South Australia, and the Learmonth solar observatory in Western Australia.

The defence minister, Richard Marles, travelled to the US last week, agreeing with the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, “to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
Marles said: “American force posture is growing in Australia, and that’s across all the domains”.
“We think that’s really important in terms of providing deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, providing for stability and peace in the Indo-Pacific, and that’s very much in Australia’s national interest.”

articles.title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
articles.summary: Mladić was jailed for genocide during the 1990s Bosnian war and the EU warned Serbia not to glorify the convicted war criminal.

blocks.text: Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.

He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.

A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral ​but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".
Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.
Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.
Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.

Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.

The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".

Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.
Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.
Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.
Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.
For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.

A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.
Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.
"He should be remembered only as a butcher."

Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.

The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."
Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.
"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

articles.title: Architect of UK’s AI policy quits after Anthropic conflict of interest concerns
articles.summary:
Matt Clifford forced to stand down amid disquiet from senior MPs over his new full-time job at AI company

The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit…

blocks.text: The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit has been forced to stand down after taking a job with the San Francisco AI firm Anthropic, after warnings from senior MPs that the move created a “clear conflict of interest”.

Matt Clifford announced last week that he was taking a full-time job working for the company behind the Claude chatbot, “leading its engagement” with governments outside the US – including the UK. But he retained his leadership at the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria), which funds frontier science and tech projects.

The move sparked concern, with Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the Commons science, innovation and technology committee, calling it a “clear conflict of interest” and outlining her disquiet in a letter to the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.
At the time Clifford’s new employer said he would recuse himself from any Anthropic-related business at Aria in an arrangement that had been agreed with the government.

Clifford announced on Monday: “I have decided to step down to ensure my new role at Anthropic doesn’t become a distraction from Aria’s incredible work.” He said he would stay in place until 6 November “with appropriate safeguards against potential conflicts in place”.

Onwurah welcomed the move but said questions remained, including “how this situation arose, what conflict of interest assessments were undertaken and what safeguards are in place to protect confidence in Aria’s governance.”

Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of government AI policy, welcomed Clifford’s resignation. “If we are to rebuild trust in the government, we need to see a clear line between tech interests and those of citizens and the nation,” she said.

Clifford’s full-time Anthropic role highlighted a revolving door between the government and AI companies. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak has taken jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft, and the former chancellor George Osborne works for OpenAI. They followed Nick Clegg, who held a senior role with Meta until 2025.

Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, had said taking extensive knowledge about a policy as sensitive as AI to a private sector company shortly after leaving government could weaken the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.

On Monday the risks of the race to ever more powerful AIs were again highlighted by the AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, who gave a statement supporting a private member’s bill being introduced on Tuesday in the UK parliament to prohibit the creation of artificial superintelligence, warning: “Losing control over AI smarter than ourselves … could even lead to human extinction.”
after newsletter promotion
Clifford was appointed Keir Starmer’s AI adviser in January 2025 but stepped down for personal reasons after six months in the role.

The 40-year-old made his career in the private sector as the co-founder of the venture capital outfit Entrepreneurs First, becoming a pivotal figure in the UK tech scene. As well taking the chair of Aria in 2022, he became a key adviser to Sunak and played a prominent role in organising the 2023 AI safety summit in the UK. He also helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.

articles.title: Netflix announces production of third Inbetweeners film
articles.summary:
Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles

Netflix has announced that production has begun on a new Inbetweeners…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: Netflix has announced that production has begun on a new Inbetweeners film, with the original cast members reprising their roles.
It will be a continuation of the popular Channel 4 sitcom, which aired on E4 from 2008 to 2010, followed by two films in 2011 and 2014.

The actors Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will star as Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper. The coming-of-age comedy followed the misadventures of the four teenage friends at the fictional Rudge Park comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship and failed sexual encounters.

The trailer announcing the new film begins with a garage door being opened and pairs of feet making their way towards a car, revealed to be Simon’s yellow Fiat Cinquecento. The four men are then seen in the car, and when it fails to start Simon says: “Ah, for fuck’s sake.”
He gets the engine going and drives the car out of the garage with the number three written on the rear windscreen. The trailer ends with the announcement: “Now in production.”

The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film. They said: “It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans.”

In the first film, which grossed £65.1m at the box office, the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post-sixth form break. It made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix.
The 2014 follow-up, which grossed £46.6m, reunited Will, Simon, and Neil as they travelled to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year.
It is not known whether Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D’Amato.

articles.title: Marcos’ critics should be silent after Romualdez’ arrest, says Lacson
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening. “With the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening.

“With the arrest of his cousin, former Speaker Romualdez, the President’s critics who have accused him of weak leadership and a lack of resolve in confronting the flood-control mess should now be silenced by his actions,” Lacson stated in a social media post.
“Let the trial proceed and let the evidence speak. Most importantly, the former Speaker is now given his day in court,” Lacson also said.

In his last State of the Nation Address, Marcos vowed that the cases against his cousin in connection with the flood control mess would still be pursued. This is amid accusations that Marcos is shielding his allies in the corruption scandal, and instead targeting the opposition.

At 7:20 p.m., Romualdez was arrested at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for plunder after supposedly receiving P7.44 billion worth of kickbacks from government projects, including flood control infrastructure from 2022 to 2025.
At around 4 p.m., hours before the news of his arrest, Romualdez was rushed to the hospital after a “cardiovascular event” and a panic attack, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.

Lacson also commended the Office of the Ombudsman, which filed the plunder case against the congressman earlier today, saying, “The Ombudsman likewise deserves all the praise and support from the Filipino people.”
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla previously characterized Romualdez as a “central figure” in the flood control mess, noting that it would be difficult to go against plentiful resources.
It was government contractors Curlee and Sarah Discaya in 2025 who first linked the former Speaker to the infrastructure anomalies.
According to the Discayas, Quezon Rep. Marvin Rillo introduced Romualdez to them as his close friend when Rillo demanded kickbacks in exchange for government contracts.

In early 2026, two witnesses linked the Discaya couple to Romualdez, alleging that a broker for a South Forbes Park home had introduced them to Curlee Discaya, who said it was the former House Speaker who bought the property.

Romualdez previously denied having any role in the flood control scheme, with his lawyers pressing that the congressman had been prejudged by the Ombudsman as a mastermind figure in the infrastructure ordeal. /cb

The city government announced this on Monday, Sept. 7, noting that the vehicles were funded by the city government through the initiative of Mayor James Bryan Alcid.
Each multipurpose vehicle is equipped with a stretcher, oxygen tank, first-aid kit, blood pressure apparatus, ladder, and chainsaw, among other equipment needed during emergencies.
The vehicles are intended to serve various barangay needs, particularly during medical emergencies, disasters and other situations requiring immediate assistance.

With the additional vehicles, barangay officials are expected to respond more quickly to emergencies and provide assistance to residents, particularly during calamities and other urgent situations. /mcm

The missing man was identified as Raul Aludos Juan, a resident of the barangay.

His disappearance was reported to the Kapangan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) around noon on Sept. 5. Barangay officials and local volunteers immediately conducted an initial search but failed to locate Juan by evening.

The municipal disaster office later activated its search and rescue team and coordinated with barangay officials, police and the Bureau of Fire Protection for operational briefings and continuing field operations.
Authorities appealed to residents to report any information that could help locate Juan.

articles.title: Russia announces it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg
articles.summary: The tit-for-tat reaction comes after Germany said it is shuttering Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural center in Berlin.

blocks.text: The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 the latest, according to Russia's Foreign Ministry.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
The move is a direct response to Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin.

Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Russia has called the idea that it is behind the attack an absurd fabrication.

articles.title: U.K. government slams 'thuggish' anti-migrant protesters, after demonstrators block port
articles.summary: The British government on Monday condemned the "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of anti-immigrant demonstrators who converged on a port in southern England where migrants were brought ashore…

image.caption: Police officers blocked anti-immigration protesters in Portsmouth, England, on Sunday, after activists blocked off a road leading to a busy ferry port. (PA Images/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The British government on Monday condemned the "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of anti-immigrant demonstrators who converged on a port in southern England where migrants were brought ashore after crossing the English Channel.
Coast guard assisted boat carrying 140 people crossing English Channel from France
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in dark clothing and wearing masks, faced off with police in Portsmouth late Sunday in an attempt to prevent lifeboats from bringing the migrants to land.
They then tried to block buses carrying the new arrivals to a processing facility for asylum seekers.
"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder," the government said in a statement.

The Portsmouth protest came a day after hundreds of masked anti-immigration protesters blocked roads leading to Britain's busiest ferry port of Dover on Saturday, clogging traffic and disrupting travellers as well as cargo vehicles heading for France .
Both groups appeared to be led by Daniel Thomas, an ally of veteran far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson.
We went on patrol with a migrant aid group on the French coast
Successive U.K. governments have struggled to stop people — more than 40,000 last year — making the dangerous journey across one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians, including Nigel Farage of the hard-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists.

items: In northern France, beaches turn to border zones as migrants wait months to cross the English Channel
A month after migrants surged into Ceuta, thousands of kids are still stranded on the streets

blocks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government says stepped-up law enforcement co-operation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 per cent compared with 2025.

The boat carrying about 140 people to Portsmouth had left early Sunday from Normandy, far west of the beaches near Calais, France, where most departures have taken place — making it a much longer and riskier journey.
Britain's Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said lifeboats, a coast guard helicopter and a plane were involved in the operation to bring the migrants to shore.

articles.title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five
articles.summary:
Theories begin to emerge that plane may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time

Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what…

blocks.text: Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what caused an Amazon cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami international airport on Sunday afternoon and crash, killing five people and injuring five others.

Video footage showed the jet wobbling a little and coming in fast and far along the runway, with storm clouds clearly visible in the sky behind, as expert theories began to emerge that the Boeing 767 may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time.

The aircraft overshot the runway around 2pm Sunday after arriving in south Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a perimeter road used by warehouse workers and other businesses before coming to rest in a parking lot. With its nose tipped forward, flames then burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air.
Authorities have not named the five who died or the five people injured, three critically, or released exact details on where the casualties were located.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said chairwoman Jennifer Homendy would hold a news conference later on Monday. US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that the agency would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.

The crash trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.

Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air, posted to social media show it touching down far along the runway. Other footage shows the plane with a left hand wheel on the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire.

Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 ft (914 meters) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot.
Some 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said.

The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando international airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning.

Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. And Amazon said in a further statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

items: The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
articles.summary: Europe just opened a carbon capture and storage plant billed as the continent's largest. But global climate scenarios call for far more capacity than exists anywhere on Earth.

image.caption: CCS targets point sources, like at this coal plant: a single smokestack where CO2 can be captured before it disperses into the atmosphereImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek/IMAGO

blocks.text: For years there has been talk of capturing and storing the carbon dioxide generated by burning fossil fuels as one way to keep the planet from overheating. In fact, the United Nations' climate science body envisions somewhere between 350 to 1,200 gigatons of CO2 storage within the century to avoid the worst effects of climate change.
But is it really happening? Yes and no.

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is an effort to trap CO2 at what's called a point source. This might be a smokestack or at an ammonia factory — in other words, a single, concentrated spot where the planet-heating greenhouse gas is emitted.
After being captured, it is compressed and transported, usually using pipelines or trains, before being stored geologically — in aquifers or old oil reservoirs, for example.

CCS is related to, but distinct from, carbon dioxide removal (CDR), which involves pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere after it's already been emitted. That CO2 is often stored similarly to CCS, but uses very different technologies for capturing.

"Given the legacy of emissions in the atmosphere, given where we are in terms of emissions reductions, we're going to need these approaches," said Wil Burns, co-director of the Institute for Carbon Removal Law & Policy at American University.
"We just have to figure out how to use them thoughtfully and still keep our eye on the prize of decarbonizing."
The technology works, but scaling is another matter
The feasibility of CCS and CDR is a subject of much debate among scientists and climate campaigners.
Advocates for scaling up the technology as a key pillar of decarbonization say the main hurdle is getting more plants built, which would require government subsidies and policy intervention.

Without governments putting a price on carbon or offering tax credits, experts say it's hard to imagine investors shelling out for these expensive commercial projects. Renewable energy, by contrast, has become so cheap over time that it's often commercially viable on its own.
"It's ready to go, technologically. We know how to do this process," said Susan Hovorka, a geoscientist at the University of Texas-Austin, researching CCS since 1998.
Carbon capture: Is it feasible?
How CCS began

CCS traces its roots back to the 1960s, when oil companies began piping natural CO2 into oil fields for enhanced oil recovery — that's where captured CO2 is injected into old oil fields to help push more oil out of the ground. It wasn't until 1996 that the first large-scale CCS project designed to reduce emissions went online in Norway.
Progress since then has been slowly ramping up. In 2020, there were 26 operational commercial CCS facilities around the world. As of last summer, the number has nearly tripled.
But others say the technology remains in its infancy, and our real-world capabilities lag far behind our technical knowhow.

"What is not well-established and basically doesn't exist at scale is the commercial experience doing this," said Danny Cullenward, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. "And proving that it works; that it's easy, that it's cost-effective, that it can be deployed at large scale, that it works in lots of different places."

Researchers from the University of Texas-Austin recently revealedthat though small-scale pilot projects have been successful in injecting CO2 into the ground, many of the world's large-scale CCS initiatives are pumping far less into storage sites than promised.

And they are not unlimited. While previous estimates put the Earth's CO2 storage capacity somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 gigatons, a new study foundthe number is just about 1,460 gigatons, meaning most CCS-reliant climate scenarios would breach the planetary limit for storage over the next 250 years.

blocks.caption: Visitors walk through the Northern Lights facility in Norway, where captured CO2 is compressed and prepared for injection thousands of meters beneath the seabedImage: Benoit Doppagne/BELGA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Climate models bet heavy on new technology

Starting this week, the European fertilizer giant Yara will open what it calls Europe's largest carbon capture project. It will harvest excess CO2 at its factory in Sluiskil Netherlands, liquefy it, and ship it to Norway's Atlantic coast to be stored in an underground rock formation, some 2,600 meters below the seabed.

That plant will only be able to capture 800,000 metric tons of CO2 annually. To meet that 350 gigaton threshold — the lower end of the UN's climate scenarios used to inform climate policy — would require about 5,800 more Yara-size plants to open tomorrow.

The International Energy Agency, another intergovernmental body that models climate data, projected7.6 gigatons of carbon will be captured every year by 2050, with almost all of it stored. Right now, the world's 77 operating plants are capable of capturing 64 million tons annually. That output would need to be multiplied by 119 over the next quarter-century to reach the IEA number.
"The scale of what's being called for in those scenarios is astronomically beyond any real activity that exists today," Cullenward said.
He says climate models tend to underestimate renewables and lean too hard on "gee-whiz" technologies.

That's because models basically have three ways to hit an ambitious climate target: add more renewables, use less energy, or bet on some new technology that solves the problem without forcing society to change much.
"If you tell a model to solve an impossible problem, it's like pouring water down a flight of stairs — it's going to find the fastest way to get to the bottom," Cullenward said.

blocks.caption: CO2 tanks at the Northern Lights storage facility where captured carbon — including from Yara's Sluiskil plant — is liquefied before being injected into a rock formation deep beneath the seabedImage: Alessandro Della Valle/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: A license to keep drilling?

One of the most contentious arguments about CCS is whether it represents a legitimate decarbonization solution or is a tactic from oil and gas companies to justify and prolong more fossil fuel extraction.

In 2023, about 80% of the world's CCS capacity was used for enhanced oil recovery, according to research and advocacy group, Oil Change International — ultimately increasing emissions and defeating CCS's climate benefit.
Some researchers also argue that CCS poses a moral hazard, or a situation where having a form of protection allows for more risk-taking.
On the other hand, advocates for the technology often talk of reserving CCS for what's called "hard-to-abate" industries, like cement.

"I don't think we're going to get to five or 10 or 20 gigatons a year of carbon removal," Cullenward said. "But we may need to get as much as we can and to me that's a reason to be more engaged rather than less engaged."
Why carbon capture needs a reality check

articles.title: Why is far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
articles.summary: Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month

blocks.text: Germany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.

blocks.caption: Alice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: What happened and why is it significant?

For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.

Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and ‌domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.

Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.
What might happen next?

The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.

Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.
What does the result say about the firewall approach?

The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.

blocks.caption: Siegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: What does the result mean for the CDU and Frederich Merz?

Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.

The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result.  Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

blocks.text: What about the next two state elections?

Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16 länder, will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.
