articles.title: Bill modernizing anti-spying law gets House OK on 2nd reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The House of Representatives on Monday approved on second reading a bill modernizing the Philippines’ decades-old anti-espionage laws by broadening their scope and applying…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The House of Representatives on Monday approved on second reading a bill modernizing the Philippines’ decades-old anti-espionage laws by broadening their scope and applying penalties in times of peace.

In a voice vote, lawmakers approved House Bill No. 9642, which expands espionage to cover the unauthorized sharing of any “classified matter” that could harm the country by giving an advantage to foreign or domestic actors.

Accessing any sketch, layout, blueprint or multimedia representation of “critical infrastructure” and national defense assets without authorization would also be considered spying, unless obtained through open sources or “other lawful means,” it added.
Violators face life imprisonment without parole and fines of up to P20 million under the measure.

The bill’s second-reading approval marks the culmination of a consolidated effort launched in 2024 to amend the country’s 84-year-old anti-espionage laws. Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. then pushed for anti-espionage reform after the arrest of a former town mayor accused of spying for China.

The Revised Penal Code defines spying as unauthorized entry into military facilities to obtain confidential information and sharing it with representatives of a “foreign power.” A 1941 Commonwealth statute defines espionage as intelligence-gathering aimed at helping enemy forces in wartime.

The measure also penalizes those who aid or abet spies, including harboring and helping them escape, with accomplices facing up to 12 years in prison and fines of as much as P20 million. If the offender is a government official, the maximum fine rises to P25 million.
Proposing and conspiring to commit espionage is also punishable by imprisonment of up to 12 years and fines of as much as P10 million under the bill.

The bill allows authorities to “secretly wiretap” suspected spies and intercept their messages upon a written order by the Court of Appeals, which also has the authority to let the Anti-Money Laundering Council examine bank accounts tied to espionage. /mcm

articles.title: Senate passes Presidential Merit Scholarship bill on final reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday passed on final reading a measure seeking to establish the Presidential Merit Scholarship Program (PMSP). Senate Bill No. 2410, or the proposed Presidential…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday passed on final reading a measure seeking to establish the Presidential Merit Scholarship Program (PMSP).
Senate Bill No. 2410, or the proposed Presidential Merit Scholarship Act, was approved with a 19-0-0 vote during Monday’s plenary session.
The bill is among the education reforms identified for priority action by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (Ledac).
Once enacted into law, it will provide educational support to academically outstanding Filipino senior high school graduates.
Scholarship benefits for eligible students will include tuition and other school fees, as well as allowances for books, cost of living and transportation.
The bill also requires scholars to render return service in the Philippines equivalent to the number of years they received scholarship assistance, beginning within one year of graduation.

Explaining his affirmative vote, Sen. Joel Villanueva, sponsor and principal author of the measure, said, “The timely release of scholarship benefits is not a request; it is an obligation of the government.”
He pointed out that late assistance to students may result in a missed semester or a lost opportunity. /mcm

articles.title: Mark Villar welcomes passage of tougher anti-hospital detention bill
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar welcomes the Senate’s approval of a bill imposing heavier penalties on hospitals and medical clinics that detain patients or their families because of unpaid…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar welcomes the Senate’s approval of a bill imposing heavier penalties on hospitals and medical clinics that detain patients or their families because of unpaid medical expenses.

The upper chamber has recently approved Senate Bill No. 1511, or the proposed Enhanced Anti-Hospital Detention Act, on third and final reading with 18 affirmative votes, no negative votes, and one abstention.
The bill seeks to strengthen Republic Act No. 9439, which prohibits hospitals and clinics from preventing patients unable to settle their medical bills immediately from going home.
“Hospitals and clinics should not become jails for our countrymen who can’t immediately pay for their bills,” Villar said in Filipino in a statement issued on Monday.
As he pointed out, hospitalization already places families under significant emotional and financial pressure. So they should not be humiliated over unpaid accounts.
Under the proposed law, hospitals and clinics found illegally detaining patients, newborn babies, or the remains of deceased patients would face heavier penalties.

The same provision also applies to patients’ relatives, representatives, and caregivers — preventing a practice known as “palit-ulo,” in which a hospital or clinic requires them to remain at the facility in exchange for the release of their patient.
It also prohibits medical facilities from withholding newborns following maternity-related treatment or refusing to release the remains of deceased patients because of unsettled hospital bills.
Under the bill, hospital employees or officers directly responsible for an illegal detention may be fined up to ₱300,000 or imprisoned for up to two years and four months.
Hospital directors or officers who create or enforce policies permitting illegal detention may face fines ranging from ₱500,000 to ₱1 million and imprisonment of four to six years.
A medical facility may also lose its license to operate after three violations committed under such a policy.

Villar clarified, however, that the measure would neither cancel legitimate medical debts nor prevent hospitals from collecting unpaid obligations. Instead, it would require healthcare facilities to use legal and humane collection methods.

Patients unable to pay their bills immediately may issue promissory notes supported by legally recognized security or guarantee arrangements. Qualified patients may also obtain guarantee letters from appropriate government agencies.

Villar acknowledged that hospitals must remain financially sustainable and have the right to collect valid debts, but stressed that financial considerations should not take precedence over a patient’s freedom and dignity. /atm

articles.title: No monitored threats vs Sara Duterte – NBI
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag on Monday said the NBI has not monitored any threat to the life of Vice President Sara Duterte. Matibag said this after…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag on Monday said the NBI has not monitored any threat to the life of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Matibag said this after Duterte on Saturday claimed that she “does not feel safe” and that she fears for her life amid an arrest warrant against her over three counts of grave threats.
Duterte arrived at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Saturday to post bail amounting to P360,000—P120,000 for each of the three counts of grave threats filed against her.
“As we speak, wala kaming namo-monitor na threat,” Matibag told reporters in an ambush interview on Monday.
(As we speak, we have not monitored any threat.)
“Kung ano ang intel report niya, we will be happy to receive it if she will share it to us,” he added.
(Whatever her intel report is, we will be happy to receive it if she will share it with us.)
Matibag said the vice president can send a letter or send someone to the bureau to report any threats to her life.
The NBI director reiterated the bureau’s mandate to protect the safety of the president, vice president, Senate president, House speaker, and chief justice.
Matibag likewise said the NBI is willing to volunteer and provide Duterte with “24/7 security.”

“We are volunteering to give her 24/7 security. The bottom line is, as the director, and in behalf of the NBI, kung merong untoward incident na mangyari sa kaniya under our care, I’m willing to be answerable personally,” Matibag said.

(We are volunteering to give her 24/7 security. The bottom line is, as the director, and on behalf of the NBI, if there is an untoward incident that happens to her under our care, I’m willing to be answerable personally.)
Meanwhile, when asked what the implications of Duterte’s statement that she “does not trust the court” would be, Matibag said he would speak as a “lawyer” and not as the “NBI director.”
“As a lawyer, that is something that is—pwede kang ma-contempt. If you are part of the bar, pwede itong maging reason for disciplinary, either suspension of your license or disbarment,” said Matibag.
(As a lawyer, that is something that is—you can be held in contempt. If you are part of the bar, it can be a reason for disciplinary action, either suspension of your license or disbarment.)

Duterte’s grave threats charges stemmed from her online press conference in November 2024, where she said that she hired a person to kill President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself is killed. /gsg

articles.title: Sara Duterte claims Marcos controls Senate, judges, police
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday told supporters not to feel “pressure” over her impeachment trial and criminal cases, expressing confidence despite claiming that President…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday told supporters not to feel “pressure” over her impeachment trial and criminal cases, expressing confidence despite claiming that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. controls the Senate, prosecutors, judges, and police.

In a statement following a series of pronouncements after an arrest warrant was issued for grave threats on Friday, Duterte thanked her supporters for their messages of support amid what she described as “relentless political harassment from the Marcos administration.”
“Many have also said that they are stressed out by the impeachment and the cases I am facing. I want to convey to all of you that you do not need to worry and do not be pressured,” she said.
“Even though Marcos controls the senators, prosecutors, judges and police, there are so many lawyers who are helping me fight and win these cases,” she added.

Duterte also claimed that the real pressure she feels is knowing that she can do only so little to help ease the public’s suffering as they wade through floodwaters, experience starvation and cope with the continued rise in the prices of basic goods.
“The real pressure is being a government official as I see that Marcos and some other officials seem to only put their own interests first, instead of the welfare of every Filipino,” she said.
Duterte was ordered arrested by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Friday for three counts of grave threats.

These charges stemmed from the alleged threats she made during a November 2024 virtual press conference against President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker and presidential cousin Martin Romualdez.
This incident also forms part of the articles of impeachment against her, apart from allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and bribery. /mcm

articles.title: Senate OKs five international resolutions on third reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved on their third and final reading five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved on their third and final reading five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher education, and taxation.
In a roll call vote, nineteen senators, with no abstentions or objections, approved the five resolutions aimed at strengthening the Philippines’ participation in international agreements;
The approved resolutions are as follows:

items: Senate Resolution No. 622, which seeks concurrence in the accession to the Protocol to Amend the Convention on Offences and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft, strengthening the legal framework for offenses committed aboard aircraft

Senate Resolution No. 624, providing concurrence in the ratification of the Philippine-India Treaty on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters, which establishes mechanisms for cooperation in investigating, prosecuting, and preventing crimes between India and the Philippines

Senate Resolution No. 625, concurring in the ratification of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, providing a framework for liability and compensation for damage caused by space objects

Senate Resolution No. 626, which seeks concurrence in the Philippines’ accession to the Asia-Pacific Regional Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications in Higher Education, facilitating the recognition of Filipino academic qualifications abroad

Senate Resolution No. 628, concurring in the ratification of the Philippines–Cambodia Agreement on the Elimination of Double Taxation and the Prevention of Fiscal Evasion with respect to Taxes on Income, which seeks to prevent double taxation and strengthen bilateral economic ties.

blocks.text: The approval of these resolutions is expected to improve the country’s cross-border cooperation while also supporting the country’s economic, educational, and security interests. /gsg

articles.title: Roblox given until October to comply with safety requirements
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Gaming platform Roblox has until October this year to comply with the requirements of establishing its office in the country and enforcing age verification through the national…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Gaming platform Roblox has until October this year to comply with the requirements of establishing its office in the country and enforcing age verification through the national ID in its system, Information and Communications Secretary Henry Aguda said on Monday.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), Aguda told lawmakers that the agency gave Roblox five demands to adhere to since May this year.
He shared that three of the five requirements have already been met.

Aguda said that Roblox already agreed to segment its platform into three: Roblox for Kids, Roblox Select, and Roblox. He noted that the gaming platform followed the agency’s instruction on the segmentation when it was called out last May.
Second, he said that Roblox already monitors chat activities of minors when it can detect conversations about sensitive topics such as sexual acts and other violent topics.
Lastly, he added that it made parental control as default in the gaming platform.
“Ang sinabi namin kay Roblox, no later than October, they should comply. There were five demands we gave to Roblox since May pa,” Aguda said.
(We told Roblox to comply [with the remaining requirements] no later than October. There were five demands we gave to Roblox since May.)
As for the requirement to build its own office in the country, Aguda shared that Roblox hired around 300 persons through its partner company.
He noted that it already built its office in Singapore with five employees, which was never done before.

The fifth requirement is for Roblox to use the country’s national ID for the age verification of gamers. In the same hearing, Aguda noted that Roblox was the one who suggested using the national ID for verification of the application users.

He added that the e-verify solution of the national ID to make the age verification more accurate, where Roblox can easily verify the player’s age with the national ID without transferring personal information to the gaming platform.
“I keep repeating Roblox kasi they can become the template for other social media platforms. Kung nagawa nila, yung iba dapat magawa rin,” he noted.
(I keep repeating Roblox kasi they can become the template for other social media platforms. If they can do it, then others can do it, too.)

Meanwhile, Aguda said that Meta committed to the enforcement aspect, which is the attribution where authorities can easily flag those who violated guidelines in social media platforms such as Facebook.
He said that Meta will bring its technical team to the country to study the integration of the national ID system to its platforms.
He also acknowledged the concerns of Meta on the technical complexity of the integration, noting that it has not been done anywhere in the world. /gsg

articles.title: Dy urges Metrobank’s Outstanding Filipinos: Uplift others, serve nation
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Use your skills and talents not only to achieve personal success but also to improve the lives of others and serve the country, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III urged the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Use your skills and talents not only to achieve personal success but also to improve the lives of others and serve the country, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III urged the awardees of the 2026 Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos, which had the theme “Beyond Excellence.”

“Excellence is being good at what you do. ‘Beyond excellence’ is when the good you do benefits others. When you go beyond the call of duty to serve our kababayans,” Dy said on Monday in his sponsorship speech for a resolution honoring the 10 awardees for their “dedication, exemplary performance, and contributions to nation-building.”
“This is beyond excellence — to go beyond what is expected of us, to give without asking in return, to value service above self.”
The Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos recognizes teachers, soldiers, and police officers who demonstrate excellence in their professions and render service beyond the call of duty.
This year’s awardees are:
Award for Teachers

items: Dr. Emmanuel D. Guarde, Master Teacher III at Cornelio Lintawagin Memorial Elementary School in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro: “Oriental Mindoro’s Steward of Indigenous Knowledge and Heritage”
Sheila Marie M. Amigo, Master Teacher I at Siay National High School in Siay, Zamboanga Sibugay: “Zamboanga Sibugay’s Trailblazer in Transformative and Compassionate Learning”
Dr. Cecilia O. Bucayong, Professor VI and director for Environmental and Safety Management at Central Mindanao University in Maramag, Bukidnon: “Bukidnon’s Visionary Inventor in Physics Education”

Dr. Jefferson A. Hora, Professor VI and dean of the College of Engineering at Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology in Iligan City, Lanao del Norte: “Mindanao’s Revolutionary Mentor in Microelectronics Education and Innovation”

blocks.text: Award for Soldiers

items: Staff Sgt. Joebelle O. Cerdinio, signal noncommissioned Officer of the 102nd Infantry Brigade, 1st Infantry Division, Philippine Army: “Zamboanga Peninsula’s Sentinel of Unified Response and Communication”
Staff Sgt. John Daren P. Noche, noncommissioned officer in charge for Safety of Tactical Operations Group 10, Philippine Air Force: “Philippine Air Force’s Innovator for Safer Communities”

Lt. Col. Rommel M. Geli, commanding officer of Marine Battalion Landing Team 9, 3rd Marine Brigade, Philippine Marine Corps: “Philippine Marine Corps’ Servant Leader in Territorial Defense and Peacebuilding”

blocks.text: Award for Police Officers

items: Police Master Sgt. Dwight Alexis B. Supsupin, team leader of the Technical Support Company, Regional Mobile Force Battalion 15, Police Regional Office Cordillera Administrative Region: “Cordillera’s Catalyst of Transformative Community Policing”

Police Maj. Baby Rose P. Cajulao, chief of the Community Affairs Section, Regional Community Affairs and Development Division, Police Regional Office 2: “Cagayan Valley’s Police Advocate for Community Empowerment”

Police Lt. Col. Robert R. Mansueto, deputy provincial director for Administration of the Antique Police Provincial Office, Police Regional Office 6: “Western Visayas’ Champion of Digital Systems for Public Safety”

blocks.text: Aim for meaningful service
Dy said the honorees showed how professional excellence could be transformed into meaningful service to the Filipino people.
“In your deeds, you have shown that excellence can be a way to serve. Talent can become caring. And one person’s success can pave the way for the majority to rise,” he said in Filipino.
He stressed that Filipinos can use their abilities to complement government programs and major policy decisions to work for the common good.

“The progress of the Philippines depends not only on big programs or decisions. It also depends on millions of Filipinos who use their abilities not only for their personal benefit but also to help us lift the people,” Dy said.

Historical figures, he pointed out, are not the only ones who have shown heroism but also “teachers who refuse to give up on their students, police officers who protect communities, soldiers who serve far from their families, and ordinary Filipinos who act even without recognition.”
“Every day, silent Filipinos doing good and heroic deeds,” Dy said.
“There are ordinary Filipinos who don’t wait for others to act. They themselves find a way to serve others — even without being seen, even without applause, even without recognition.”
He urged the awardees to continue inspiring other Filipinos to pursue excellence with compassion and a sense of responsibility toward others.

“Because the Philippines we want to build will be shaped by millions of Filipinos choosing to do their part for the benefit of others. Let’s make our excellence more meaningful by making positive changes in the lives of others,” he said.
“May you continue using your excellence to serve, give hope, and open opportunities for more of our countrymen.” /atm

articles.title: Romualdez suffers from ‘cardiovascular event, panic attack’ – Remulla
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez suffered a “cardiovascular event” and a purported panic attack, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Monday…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez suffered a “cardiovascular event” and a purported panic attack, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Monday night.
Romualdez was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City around 4 p.m. on Monday, Remulla said in an interview with reporters.
“According to the doctors, he’s suffered from a cardiovascular event. His blood pressure was unstable and he was having an anxiety attack,” Remulla explained.
“The Philippine National Police’s doctors are here to determine his status in conference with his doctors,” he added.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered the Leyte 1st District representative taken into government custody.

Romualdez was charged by the Office of the Ombudsman before the Sandiganbayan on Monday for allegedly receiving P7.44 billion worth of kickbacks from flood control, infrastructure and other government projects from 2022 to 2025.
“We will check every day until he is well enough to be presented to the court,” Remulla said.
“We assure you, he cannot hide behind his wealth. No matter how rich he is, he cannot pay the law to allow him to stay in a place of this caliber. This isn’t a permanent situation,” he added.

“His room in Payatas is just waiting if the court commits him. The fight is fair here,” he stressed, referring to the New Quezon City Jail, where other personalities allegedly involved in the infrastructure corruption scandal have been jailed.
Remulla did not say when Romualdez would undergo booking procedures.
This is a developing story. /mcm

articles.title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
articles.summary:
Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and…

blocks.text: A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US.

Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged.

Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states.

Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end.

Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group.

Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorney generals and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts.

In response, the DoJ’s solicitor general John Sauer on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”.

On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”

In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS has been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting.
About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports.

With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former DoJ lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.

Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.”

Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.”

Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption.

Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and nonpartisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.”

Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting.

For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG.

blocks.caption: A Kentucky voter in Louisville casts her ballot. Photograph: Bryan Woolston/Reuters

blocks.text: Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU has been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made.

Critics say Trump, the DoJ, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules.

In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year.

Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century.

But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”.
The DoJ has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions.

In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”.
In August, the DoJ announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation.

And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the DoJ’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation.
Former DoJ lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial.

Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-DoJ lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections.

“The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.”

Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.
Other DoJ alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical.

“These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DoJ inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.”

Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes.

“Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.”

Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it has teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections.

Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and Daga’s litigation against it.

He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.”
Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the DoJ’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail.

She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.”
Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail.

Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.”

articles.title: DepEd seeks more funds as ARAL gets zero in proposed 2027 budget
articles.summary: The Department of Education is requesting an additional P145 billion in 2027 to fund the ARAL Program, hire new teachers, build classrooms, and improve students' health, among others

blocks.text: BUDGET BRIEFING. Education Secretary Sonny Angara presents the proposed P976-billion budget of the Department of Education and its attached agencies during a House appropriations committee hearing on September 7, 2026.
Department of Education
The Department of Education is requesting an additional P145 billion in 2027 to fund the ARAL Program, hire new teachers, build classrooms, and improve students' health, among others

items: The proposed 2027 budget for the Department of Education has no allocation for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning Program.
The DepEd is seeking additional funds totaling P145.19 billion, including P15.98 billion specifically for the ARAL Program.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program has no allocation in the proposed 2027 budget, according to Education Secretary Sonny Angara, potentially hurting efforts of the Department of Education (DepEd) to address the learning crisis in the country.

“There’s a zero allotment for this under the 2027 budget,” Angara told the House appropriations committee on Monday, September 7, when asked regarding the proposed allocation for the national learning intervention program next year.
The ARAL Program, institutionalized through Republic Act (RA) No. 12028 in October 2024, seeks to help public school students who struggle in reading, mathematics, and science.

With the program’s funding scrapped in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), the DepEd presented its “wishlist” to lawmakers on Monday. Part of the department’s request is P15.98 billion to carry out the ARAL Program in 2027.
In the 2026 national budget, the program was allocated P8.9 billion.

“The program has good results because out of the 6.67 million students that entered the ARAL Program, we saw at the end of the [previous] school year (2025-2026) that there were 4.5 million fewer struggling readers, with 2.5 million students improving to grade-level reading,” Angara said in a mix of English and Filipino.

blocks.caption: Most Grade 11 students struggle with reading. What now?

blocks.text: So far, the DepEd has only rolled out learning interventions for reading, according to Angara. He hopes they can include sessions for mathematics and science.

Ruby Bernardo, Alliance of Concerned Teachers national chairperson, expressed dismay over the possible zero budget for the ARAL Program. She also stressed that remediation and learning recovery efforts must already be removed from teachers’ load.

“Kung mananatili ‘yan sa teachers natin, malaki ang epekto niya sa learning recovery ng mga bata. Kung walang pondo, wala ring maha-hire na external tutors,” Bernardo said in a chance interview. (If the task would remain with the teachers, it would have a huge effect on the learning recovery of children. If there’s no funding, there would be no hiring of external tutors.)
Angara sought intervention from lawmakers as RA 12028 is specific that teachers are only entitled to overload pay if they exceed six hours of teaching.
This is amid the unresolved issue of whether teachers should be compensated for handling ARAL tutor work regardless of teaching load.

Angara said that for now, the DepEd is studying the possibility of giving food allowance in cash, if allowed by the Commission on Audit. The agency is also eyeing to include in the six-hour teaching load some teacher-related tasks, such as the time spent on peer-mentoring sessions or advising students.

In a message to Rappler, Karol Mark Yee, executive director of the Second Congressional Commission for Education, said he hopes that Congress will fund the ARAL Program as it is an “urgent need,” given that there are millions of struggling readers.
But Yee also noted that there must be a thorough review of the DepEd’s utilization of the nearly P9-billion ARAL Program funding this year.
In the 2027 NEP, the DepEd, including its attached agencies, may get P976 billion. However, the education department received P1 trillion in the 2026 budget.

blocks.caption: DepEd asks for P976-billion budget for 2027

blocks.text: In total, the DepEd requested from the House appropriations committee P145.19 billion in additional funds, while its attached agencies are seeking P1.74 billion more.
The additional funds being sought include P33.53 billion for new personnel. According to Angara, the proposed 2027 budget does not have an allocation for the hiring of new teachers.
Angara also lamented the proposed P11-billion budget for the school-based feeding program, a significant decrease from the P25.7 billion in the 2026 budget.
He explained that the feeding cycle might have to be shortened from 180 days to 120 days, and the lower budget would prevent the DepEd from offering universal feeding to all Grade 1 pupils.
Measures to address school violence, such as strengthening school safety and expanding access to mental health services, are also covered by the budget requests.

When asked how the budget cuts could affect the DepEd’s reforms, Angara told reporters after the seven-hour budget hearing, “It would slow it down a little bit, but we are hoping for a restoration of some of the items.”

articles.title: DepEd’s 2027 spending plan becoming ‘discretionary’ budget — watchdog
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A budget watchdog warned on Monday that the Department of Education’s (DepEd) proposed spending plan for next year is becoming a “discretionary, centrally pooled” budget. In a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A budget watchdog warned on Monday that the Department of Education’s (DepEd) proposed spending plan for next year is becoming a “discretionary, centrally pooled” budget.

In a statement, the Amplify Education Budget Initiative observed that some line items in DepEd’s proposed budget have been merged, including voucher programs and school facilities funding, muddling transparency and civil society oversight.

“Vouchers, inclusive-education funds, and school-building money that once carried regional shares or stood as their own line items are now pooled in the Central Office, with no published list of what will be built or bought,” it said.
The group warned that the agency’s central office would hold outsized discretion “over tens of billions of pesos,” a trend it said was worrying as the nation heads into an election cycle in 2028.
“When the same money is merged into a broad Central Office pool, that trail goes dark, and the choice of who benefits shifts from a transparent formula to an official’s discretion,” it said.

Some previously separate line items have now been merged into one, including the voucher program for senior high school students in the academic and trade tracks and the Educational Service Contracting project for junior high school students.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara told reporters that the agency was prompted to combine the three programs for budget flexibility.
“Without a special provision, you cannot transfer unused funds,” he said in Filipino.
DepEd’s voucher programs aim to subsidize tuition for students enrolling in private schools as part of its efforts to ease congestion in public classrooms.

“Merging three separate entitlements into one pooled line obscures how much reaches each type of learner and removes the per-program guardrails that let Congress and the public hold each subsidy to account,” the Amplify Education Budget Initiative said.

How DepEd’s line-item proposal for the voucher programs was presented caused confusion during the agency’s Monday budget hearing, as Caloocan Rep. Edgar Erice asked why a specific voucher program was zeroed out for next year.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara clarified during Monday’s budget hearing that funding for subsidy projects was consolidated into a single line, with that program facing a P3 billion cut.
“It’s reduced a bit, so that means [fewer] beneficiaries also,” he told lawmakers in mixed English and Filipino.
Those initiatives, now consolidated under the Government Assistance and Subsidies program, were earmarked P38.1 billion for next year.

A copy of DepEd’s 2027 spending plan showed that the program had safeguards for disbursement, including a regular spending review by the State Assistance Council and publication of the list of participating schools on the agency’s website.

The watchdog also raised concerns that funding for DepEd’s indigenous peoples education program and Madrasah program was lodged at the agency’s central office instead of the regional offices closest to the communities. /mcm

articles.title: Padilla floats community service for poor parents under social media ban
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Robin Padilla on Monday floated the idea of imposing community service, such as sweeping the streets of Quezon City, on poor parents once the proposed social media ban for…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Robin Padilla on Monday floated the idea of imposing community service, such as sweeping the streets of Quezon City, on poor parents once the proposed social media ban for children below 16 years old becomes law.

Padilla, chairman of the Senate committee on public information, was defending Senate Bill No. 2424 on the Senate floor when Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked about the penalties for parents of those found violating the proposed law.

“Hindi po ba dapat i-increase natin yung penalty for parents? Nakikita ko rito penalty, P5,000. Baka tawanan lang tayo ng mga magulang pagka ang mga penalty natin ay P5,000, but not more than P50,000,” Sotto said.
(Shouldn’t we increase the penalty for parents? I see here that the penalty is P5,000. Parents might just laugh at us if the penalty is only P5,000, but not more than P50,000.)
“Baka pwede po nating pag-aralan. Eh kung papayag po kayo sa period of amendments magpo-propose po ako ng mas mabigat-bigat nang konti sa bulsang penalty sa mga magulang para matakot,” he added.
(Perhaps we could study this further. If you agree, during the period of amendments, I can propose a slightly heavier penalty for parents so that it would serve as a deterrent.)
Padilla quickly agreed with the suggestion.

“Opo, napakaganda po nyang mga inyo pong suhestyon,” he said. “Maaari lang po natin sigurong bigyan ng katumbas na community service. Halimbawa po kung mahirap po yung magulang, pantayan po natin ng community service. Pagwalisin po natin ng buong Quezon City, mga ganun po.”

(Yes, that is a very good suggestion,” he said. “Perhaps we could provide for an equivalent community service. For example, if the parent is poor and cannot afford the penalty, we could impose community service instead. We could have them sweep and clean the streets throughout Quezon City, something along those lines.)
Sotto chuckled and said: “Baka abutin ng isang taon yan.”
That might take a year.)

Aside from a fine of not less than P5,000 but not more than P50,000, parents and guardians of social media ban violators would also be required to attend digital parenting and child online safety programs, as provided for in the bill.
“No penalty shall be imposed on parents or guardians for mere failure of supervision absent proof of willful intent or gross negligence,” it further reads.
Meanwhile, a fine of up to P20 million per violation awaits any social media platform or third-party age assurance provider found to be in violation of the proposed measure.

The amount is on top of a daily fine of up to P100,000 “for continuing violations until full compliance is achieved” or possible “suspension, restriction, or revocation of operations, permits, or access within the Philippines for repeated, willful, or gross violations, subject to due process.”
Even those figures were small compared with the $18 billion that Meta was ordered to pay in the United States, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian pointed out.

“Kaya po yung penalty na sinasabi ng ating former Senate President na P1 million, parang ano lang ito, walang masyadong epekto sa kanila dahil billion dollars po ang pinag-uusapan sa America,” Gatchalian said.

(That’s why the P1 million penalty being proposed by our former Senate President may not have much of an impact on them, considering that we are talking about billions of dollars in the United States.)
Under the bill, no child below 16 years old should “register for, access, use, maintain, operate and create on any age-restricted social media platform.”

Access may only be permitted for legitimate educational purposes and if certified by the Department of Education, Commission on Higher Education or Technical Education and Skills Development Authority.
Children aged 16 to 18, on the other hand, may access and use age-restricted social media platforms subject to age assurance requirements and child safety measures established under the bill.
In the House of Representatives, a prohibition on the use of social media is being sought for children below 13 years old, while restrictions are being proposed for those aged 13 to 18. /mcm

articles.title: Elon Musk thanked by German far-right leader after landmark election win praised by Russia | First Thing
articles.summary: Populist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD wins vote in eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Plus, 50 years since The Muppet Show first hit our screens

blocks.text: Good morning. A far-right leader who has won an important state election in Germany has thanked Elon Musk for his support, as voices in Europe warn the result is a serious moment for the continent. No far-right party has led or formed a government in Germany since the defeat of nazism at the end of the second world war.

Ulrich Siegmund, the Alternative für Deutschland’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X after the tech billionaire said “Well done!” in German to the AfD co-founder Alice Weidel. The populist, far-right, anti-immigration party won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

During its campaign, the AfD sought to capitalise on a mood of nostalgia for the communist East Germany and discontent among east Germans. The party has promised a remigration and deportation offensive, to ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. It wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and reintroduce the singing of the country’s national anthem in schools.

items: Will the AfD be able to form a state government? Despite its resounding victory, the party fell just short of a majority. It was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called “firewall” of the mainstream parties, which refuse to work with it. The final results showed the AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member legislature.

What has been the reaction in Washington and Moscow? Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection without comment on his Truth Social site. The Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians in Germany to no longer receive refugee status.

blocks.text: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, former US defense secretary warns

blocks.caption: Leon Panetta said the Iran conflict risked becoming another ‘forever war in the Middle East’. Photograph: Paul Buck/EPA

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, the former US defense secretary Leon Panetta has said, adding that it risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.

“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.

items: Who else has been saying Trump’s war may not achieve its aims? The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said on Sunday morning Washington might not be able to reach an agreement with Tehran that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock

blocks.caption: The case against Lindsay Clancy has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon. Photograph: Greg Derr/Reuters

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and the millions watching on were back where they started after her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial. The case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped the US and the world.

items: What will Clancy’s defense team most likely do? They will almost certainly push to have the charges against their client dropped, aggressively lobby against another trial and make a case to the district attorney’s office along the lines of: “Why are you doing this to this poor woman? She’s still clearly obviously suffering. She’s been punished with her paralysis and, worse than that, the loss of her three children.”

blocks.text: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

blocks.caption: There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters

blocks.text: Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk former lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

articles.title: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
articles.summary: Hafidh Ameir Hassan kept a low profile and was rarely seen in public with the president.

blocks.text: The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.
Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.
Ndejembi added that funeral arrangements are under way in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar.
Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.
In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.
The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.
Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow".
"President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.
Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".
The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.
He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.
Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.

blocks.text: Arrest warrant issued vs Romualdez, Co, 2 others over plunder

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division on Monday issued an arrest warrant against former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez, former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co and two others over their plunder case.
Once arrested, they would stay behind bars since plunder is a non-bailable offense.
Earlier, the Office of the Ombudsman filed the information which contains the formal charges against Romualdez.

According to the information containing the formal charges filed by prosecutors before the anti-graft court, Romualdez and Co were charged for “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages. kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.
Aside from Co, also charged were Romualdez’s staff Jocelyn Sereño and a certain Felecito Guevarra, president of a money changing firm.

“The issuance of a warrant of arrest signifies only that, after personally evaluating the records, the Court found probable cause to believe that the accused committed the offense charged,” the Third Division said in a statement.

“Probable cause for the issuance of a warrant of arrest exists when the facts and circumstances alleged by the prosecution would lead a reasonably discreet and prudent person to believe that an offense has been committed by the person sought to be arrested,” the court said.
“It does not constitute a determination of guilt.”
Aside from the arrest warrant, the Third Division also issued a hold departure order against all accused. /gsg

articles.title: NBI chief to Romualdez: It’s better for you to surrender
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — It will be better for Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez to surrender, National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag said on Monday, noting that the bureau…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — It will be better for Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez to surrender, National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag said on Monday, noting that the bureau will locate him as soon as they receive his warrant of arrest.

Matibag said this after the Office of the Ombudsman filed plunder raps against Romualdez, as well as former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Elizaldy Co., and several other co-accused before the Sandiganbayan, regarding the alleged flood control anomalies.
Plunder is a nonbailable offense.
“It’s better na mag-surrender kaysa magkaroon pa ng incident ng arrest,” Matibag said in an ambush interview on Monday afternoon.
(It’s better for him to surrender than to have another incident of arrest.)
“Wala naman tayong ibang pupuntahan eh. Mahirap pong magtago sa kamay ng batas. Mahaba po kamay ng batas, eventually aabutan po tayo,” he also said.
(We have nowhere else to go. It’s hard to hide from the law. The arm of the law is long.)
Matibag said the NBI will immediately dispatch a team to locate and arrest the former House speaker.
When asked how many personnel would be deployed to conduct the arrest, Matibag said it would “not that many.”
“One division per area (Romualdez’s reported location). Hindi naman ganoon kadami. We don’t want to do an overkill,” he said.
(One division per area. It’s not that many. We don’t want to do an overkill.)

Romualdez and Co are accused of “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments,’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. said during his fifth State of the Nation Address in July that the Ombudsman is preparing to file charges against his cousin.
Romualdez, in response, said he “respects” Marcos’ remarks but noted that he is ready to prove his innocence. /gsg

articles.title: 26 Filipino seafarers awaiting repatriation after Ukraine attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said in a statement Monday.
The DMW said that as of Sept. 4, the 26 Filipino seafarers safely disembarked from the vessel. The seafarers are currently awaiting transit to Moldova before their repatriation to the Philippines.

The DMW said it is coordinating with the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Philippine Embassy in Warsaw, Philippine Consulate General in Kyiv and Migrant Workers Office (MWO) in Prague to monitor the seafarers’ condition and facilitate their “safe and immediate” return, including the processing of their travel documents with Moldovan authorities and the ship owner.
Labor Attaché Llewelyn Perez said the Philippine diplomatic posts were working with Moldovan authorities and the shipowner to complete the documents needed for the crew’s return.

“The Philippine Embassy and the Philippine Consulate in Kyiv are coordinating with the relevant authorities, in partnership with the shipowner, to facilitate the processing of their travel documents,” Perez said.
The DMW said it is also coordinating with the licensed manning agency and the ship owner to address the seafarers’ immediate needs following their disembarkation.

“The DMW assures the families of the affected seafarers that it, together with its MWOs, Philippine embassies, and consulates, is facilitating the necessary arrangements for their safe return to the Philippines.” /gsg

articles.title: ‘Nakedly political’: US attempts to link trans support to authoritarianism in new HHS report
articles.summary:
HHS releases report linking ‘gender ideology’ to political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a

blocks.text: The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a report linking “gender ideology” to leftwing authoritarianism and political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted and “nakedly political”, likely leading to greater politicization of science and health.

It follows attempts by the administration to limit access to gender-affirming care – including, on Friday, an agreement reached between the Department of Justice and a New York hospital to no longer offer pediatric gender-affirming care. Dozens of hospitals stopped offering gender-affirming care after the Trump administration began investigating them for offering the standard of care.

Patients on Medicaid and government insurance plans have also been blocked from accessing care, and a proposed rule would block any health system offering gender-affirming care from receiving federal funding.

The new report, which was not published by a scientific journal and did not undergo peer review, takes aim at medical organizations offering guidelines on gender-affirming care. It also links those who say they support trans individuals with supporting authoritarianism and political violence.

“It was a very poorly done piece of research,” said Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, an epidemiologist from the University of Sydney, who highlighted several methodological failings. “It was nakedly political. I think this is probably the most obviously political study that I’ve come across.”
The report is “quite an abnormal document with a number of oddities,” said Daniel Aaron, an associate professor at the University of Utah’s SJ Quinney College of Law.

“It likely also violates federal law because it’s not peer-reviewed, and it’s essentially quite an influential dissemination of information,” which could mean it violates the Information Quality Bulletin, a federal regulation that requires peer review for influential scientific information from the US government, he said.
The HHS did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about whether this report was commissioned by the agency and if it violated federal regulations.
Aaron believes the report would not survive peer review and wondered why a political science report was published by HHS.
“It’s actually not even health-related, so I don’t understand why this is related to HHS’s mission,” Aaron said.

Craig Konnoth, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law who coauthored with Aaron a perspective on gender-affirming care policy for the New England Journal of Medicine, agreed. He sees the report as an attempt to undermine mainstream health and science organizations such as the American Psychological Association, American Psychiatric Association, the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, and the American Academy of Pediatrics, all named in the report.

“By that standard, any medical recommendation becomes ‘authoritarian’. Any standard set by any licensing board becomes ‘authoritarian’,” Konnoth said. “What we’re seeing is this broadside attack on the scientific establishment more generally, and trans rights are being used as the vehicle to do this.”

Colin Wright, an author of the report and a fellow at the conservative thinktank Manhattan Institute, said he believes the study was published by HHS quickly because a draft had been leaked to the public. He said the researchers are planning to release more information, including the numbers from the survey, and they are planning to submit the study to an unnamed journal for publication.
“It was kind of a surprise to us that it dropped when it did, and so we didn’t have plans beforehand,” Wright said. “We probably could have tightened the language a little bit more.”

Wright disputed that the study was an attempt to link support for trans people and political authoritarianism and violence, though the report itself says: “These findings suggest that gender ideology is associated with LWA [left-wing authoritarianism] and willingness to justify political violence.” Gender ideology was measured by statements such as: “People should be supported in expressing their transgender identity,” and “Parents should support their children’s transgender exploration.”

Wright suggested that the study is about the guidance offered by medical organizations and “in many ways geared to make people sort of have a more extreme reaction to it, and to kind of fuel somewhat authoritarian tendencies of trying to silence people” on gender-affirming care. He argued that the guidelines appear to push people toward ideological extremes.
“Sort of independently, it increased their willingness, at least correlationally, to their support for political violence,” Wright said. “There’s a lot of ideological content to it.”
In an online survey, 1,208 people ranked statements about support for trans people as well as about political ideology and political violence.

The political ideology questionnaire essentially measured whether someone was a Democrat, said Meyerowitz-Katz, who added: “I don’t think anyone would think this is a good measure of authoritarianism.”

One of the statements was about whether opposition to gay marriage is homophobic; another was a statement about whether the focus on terrorism should shift to the far right. “If you were a rational human being who understood the facts, you would agree with that,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. For instance, approximately 75-80% of deaths from terrorist attacks in the United States come from people on the far right, and rightwing attacks are more lethal than leftwing violence.

Similarly, the questions on political violence focused only on political violence against conservative figures or institutions, he said. If they’d included political violence against other actors, “you would almost certainly see the opposite correlation,” making the questionnaire an unreliable predictor of whether someone supports political violence, Meyerowitz-Katz said.

It was also difficult to parse these relationships, because the researchers haven’t yet released any numbers from the survey, Meyerowitz-Katz said: “The only thing they report in that paper is correlations.” But they don’t say, for instance, how many respondents supported actions like arson of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) buildings.
“This is very silly,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. “They’re producing what I would describe as pseudoscience … It’s a bad, poorly done report.”

Konnoth, who studies the link between opposition to LGBT rights and authoritarianism, noted that the report overlooks significant research in the field. “They don’t cite and engage in the data that goes against that thesis,” he said.
Typically, HHS publishes issue briefs and synthesized information, but this is an “extremely weird” case of the HHS appearing to adopt a study as its own report, Aaron said.

The purpose of the report appears to be an attempt to correlate leftwing people, particularly those who support transgender people, with violence, said Meyerowitz-Katz. “The only possible outcome of this survey was to show a correlation between leftwing beliefs and support for transgender people and ‘political violence’, and so I think that was the aim. I don’t see another possible way to interpret this particular piece of research.”

Aaron said it appears to be “aimed to benefit a political group or demonize an opposing group and build political support,” he said. “It kind of builds this fake evidence base for transgender people as a political issue.”

HHS is tasked with protecting the health and wellbeing of all Americans, he said, noting: “It’s not happening here.” Aaron compared the report with recent actions on vaccines that depart from the scientific evidence and reshape the vaccine infrastructure – influencing those who make decisions on vaccines and fueling the anti-vaccine political movement.
“I think we can draw parallels with this consistent anti-science production of information by the federal government,” he said.
Konnoth called it an “attempt to create an alternate scientific narrative” that affects all Americans.

“There’s a targeting of these mainstream fundamental organizations that put out research that doesn’t just involve trans rights, but involves broader claims about science,” he said. “If we buy into their attempt to discredit the medical establishment, then we are in deep trouble … It’s life-and-death for massive swathes of the American population.”

articles.title: US labor unions saw membership gains in 2025, mostly in states with bargaining protections
articles.summary:
Uptick in US union membership coincides with high public approval ratings of unions

After years of decline, union membership in the US increased by 411,000 members in 2025, the largest…

blocks.text: After years of decline, union membership in the US increased by 411,000 members in 2025, the largest increase since 2008, according to a new report.
The report makes clear the impact that “right to work” laws can have on union membership: most gains were concentrated in states that protect collective bargaining.

Union membership rates in those states were nearly triple than the 26 states with so-called “right-to-work” laws that weaken union membership, according to the report from the Illinois Economic Policy Institute (ILEPI) and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

States with collective bargaining protections saw an increase of nearly 305,000 union members in 2025, compared to about 107,000 in “right-to-work” states. States with protections have over 10.9 million members out of 76.9 million workers, compared to “right-to-work” states that have 3.7 million members out of 69.7 million workers.

“Right-to-work” laws allow workers to “free ride”, or work under a collectively bargained contract agreement without paying union membership dues. Most right-to-work legislation was passed in the 1940s and 1950s after a movement from conservative activist Vance Muse, who coined the term and championed it in southern states with arguments to preserve Jim Crow-era laws.

“The data consistently shows that workers earn higher wages when they are union members and work in states that protect collective bargaining rights,” said Frank Manzo IV, economist at the ILEPI and coauthor of the report. “More Americans are turning to unions as a bulwark against the rising cost of living..”

In 2025, 19 US states passed 88 laws that expanded workers’ rights, according to a 3 September issue brief by State Futures and NYU Wagner Labor Initiative. Legislation included paid sick leave and medical leave passed in Virginia, warehouse worker protections passed in Connecticut and banning nearly all non-compete agreements in Washington.

Earlier reports had shown that 2025 was a big year for unions: 16.5 million workers were represented by unions in 2025, the highest level recorded in 16 years, accounting for 11.2% of all wage and salary workers in the US. Union density, or the percentage of workers in a union, increased from 9.9% to 10.0% nationally in 2025.

The uptick in union membership coincides with high public approval ratings of unions. According to a recently released Gallup poll, 71% of Americans approve of labor unions and 47% want unions to have more influence.

Ahead of Labor Day, the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, released poll results that found 52% of the American public said they trust labor unions, compared to 32% who said they trust Democratic party and 26% who trust the Republican party.
The poll also found young workers trust unions at higher rates, with 57% of young workers who are not in a union stating that they would join one if it were an option.

“This Labor Day, shit’s too expensive,” said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, during an address last week ahead of Labor Day. “That’s what 94% of workers told us, in our new poll. Four out of five say: paychecks aren’t keeping up with the cost of living – groceries, rent, childcare, gas. This is happening, by the way, in a country where CEOs now make an average of 312 times what the median worker makes. CEOs got a 21% raise in one year – who else gets that?”

Researchers of the new report found that labor unions raise average wages by 8% nationally and workers in states that protect collective bargaining rights earn 8% more, after accounting for cost of living differences, than those in states with restrictions. Workers in these states also experienced 3% slower wage growth from 2019 to 2025.

This wage gap between workers in states with protections versus those without has more than doubled over the past decade, from 3.2% in 2015 to 6.7% in 2025, translating to over $4,000 less per year for the median full-time worker.

“By raising the wage floor, collective bargaining benefits union and non-union workers alike,” said Robert Bruno, professor at University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and director of the Project for Middle Class Renewal. “The data makes clear that a rising tide lifts all boats.”
