articles.title: Dominican Republic's Joheirry Mola Dominguez crowned Miss World 2026
articles.summary: The Miss World pageant has crowned its queen for its 75th anniversary, with Joheirry Mola Dominguez of the Dominican Republic emerging victorious over 110 other delegates. Dominguez succeeded…

blocks.text: The Miss World pageant has crowned its queen for its 75th anniversary, with Joheirry Mola Dominguez of the Dominican Republic emerging victorious over 110 other delegates.
Dominguez succeeded Thailand’s Opal Suchata Chuangsri as Miss World after winning the title at the culmination of the competition at April 2 Square in Nha Trang, Vietnam, on Sept. 5.
She is the second Miss World winner of her country, after Mariasela Alvarez crowned in 1982, or 44 years ago.
During the question-and-answer portion, Dominguez was asked: Which beauty with a purpose goals have you supported in your country, and how would you grow it if you were crowned Miss World?

Her answer: “My beauty with a purpose is to take English programs to kids in vulnerable communities because I believe that when they know this language, the opportunities, the doors that can open in their lives, it’s huge, big doors. Because I was talking to the girls and telling them that, thanks to that tool, we are here. We have the tool to express our feelings, to express our purpose, and for me, it’s something that I will take always in my heart that I could give those kids something very important, a tool that’s going to work for the rest of their lives.”
Two more delegates garnered podium placements. Elisabeth Reynés Alabern from Spain was proclaimed first runner-up, while Taanusiya Chetty from Malaysia finished as second runner-up.
Three more ladies made it to the final round of the competition—Le Nguyen Bao Ngoc from Vietnam, Snit Habteab Tewoldemedhin from Eritrea, and Romanda Hombir from South Africa.

Rain interrupted the ceremony, after the delegatea from the second group of delegates from Africa were presented. April 2 Square is an outdoor venue, and there was no roof over the stage and the audience area.
After more than half an hour, the rain stopped and the program resumed with the delegates from Europe, followed by the participants from Asia and Oceania.
The Philippine’s Asia Rose Simpson finished in the Top 12, being the second top performer from Asia and Oceania. She was edged out of the continental Top 6 by the host delegate.

Simpson earned her Top 40 placement ahead of the final competition for being the “Head-to-Head” Challenge winner for the Asia and Oceania group. She was also the overall challenge winner, sending her straight to the Top 20.

Megan Young remains to be the lone Filipino woman to bring home the Miss World crown. She scored the Philippines’ first-ever victory at the 63rd edition of the international pageant held in Indonesia in 2013.
The coronation night served as the culmination of the 73rd edition of the Miss World pageant, celebrating its 75th anniversary. It was the first time for Vietnam to host the international pageant.

articles.title: US envoys outlined 'number of ideas' on ending Ukraine war - Kremlin
articles.summary: US envoys put forward ‘number of ideas’ on Ukraine to Putin: Kremlin MOSCOW – US envoys proposed a “number of ideas” on how to end the Ukraine war in “frank”…

blocks.text: US envoys put forward ‘number of ideas’ on Ukraine to Putin: Kremlin

MOSCOW – US envoys proposed a “number of ideas” on how to end the Ukraine war in “frank” talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin late Saturday, Moscow said, ahead of their first trip to Kyiv.

US President Donald Trump’s business partner Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met Putin for more than three hours, the Kremlin said, as Washington tries to revive negotiations to end Europe’s worst conflict since WWII.

Their visit to Moscow comes after the war — which has killed hundreds of thousands and forced millions to flee their homes — escalated this summer. It also follows a visit last month to Moscow by the director of the CIA director.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks “extremely frank”, saying the Americans “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, but did not elaborate.
The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was “confident” it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added.
It was Kushner and Witkoff’s eighth visit to Moscow during the war — but it will be their first in the Ukrainian capital, hit by deadly Russian strikes throughout the war.
Both Russia and Ukraine have vowed not to strike each others’ capitals for three days to allow for the negotiations to take place.
Envoys fly out
In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv — a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war.
“We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
A day earlier, Kyiv said Russia had struck the headquarters of its SBU security services in the city’s historic centre with a drone.
Russia’s TASS news agency reported the Americans had flown out of Moscow.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was expecting the envoys on Sunday and it was unclear how they would get to Kyiv by then.
Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war in February 2022 and visiting leaders have been arriving by train.
Putin thanks Trump
Earlier Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war — launched by Russia in 2022 — despite it being “not simple”.
Of the envoys’ trip to Kyiv, he said: “No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial.”
Trump said on Friday his envoys were bringing a “proposal” on ending fighting.
“We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating.
Moscow occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine. Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of east Ukraine.
Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow after a summer of escalation that saw a drastic rise in civilian deaths on both sides.
Kyiv said Saturday that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country Saturday — including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv.
Limited truce
Both Moscow and Kyiv have said they would halt strikes on each others cities to allow for negotiations.
“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky — who had offered a truce during the US visits — later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelensky said.
On Saturday, Putin said he had “noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced” its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war — which has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
As peace efforts stalled, in part because of Washington’s war with Iran, Moscow and Kyiv stepped up their long-range attacks.
Russian strikes
As the US envoys were in the Kremlin, Ukraine said Russian attacks had killed three members of the same family in the city of Chuguiv in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
“As a result of this shelling, almost the entire family was killed: a 19-year-old girl, an 11-year-old boy, and a 45-year-old man,”regional leader Oleg Synegubov said.
Earlier Saturday, Russia struck Kyiv’s suburbs and in the Dnipro region, where local officials said five people had been killed.
Zelensky accused Moscow of trying to disrupt the visit of the US envoys with overnight attacks on Kyiv’s two airports — as well as on the civilian targets.

articles.title: Drone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in Colombia
articles.summary:
Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound

An attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a…

blocks.text: An attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a military compound in north-eastern Colombia has killed at least three soldiers and wounded four, Colombia’s army said on Saturday.
Local authorities blamed the attack – which took place late on Friday – on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN).

It targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela. Two soldiers died at the site and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia’s military said on X.

Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, condemned the attack. “For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the state down upon the criminals,” he said.

Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbours dissident factions of the now defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.
Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia’s primary coca-producing areas.
In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN.
Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in north-eastern Colombia.

articles.title: Sara Duterte posts bail: ‘I don’t trust the court’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail before a Quezon City court, securing her provisional liberty a day after a warrant was issued for her arrest on…
articles.byline: Holly Kylie Merian C. Bacay, Kathleen de Villa

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail before a Quezon City court, securing her provisional liberty a day after a warrant was issued for her arrest on charges that she issued grave threats against President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.

Duterte appeared before Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) shortly before 11 a.m., accompanied by lawyers Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim. Bail was set at P120,000 for each of the three counts of the charge.
But what was supposed to be a routine legal proceeding saw the accused—who was haled to court for what she said in a fit of rage—becoming the one expressing fears for her safety.
‘I do not feel safe’

The case stems from Duterte’s remarks during an online press conference on Nov. 23, 2024, when she said she had spoken to someone about killing Marcos, the first lady and Romualdez if she herself were killed.
Duterte has denied the allegations.
The same remarks form part of the impeachment case now pending before the Senate.
Before entering the Hall of Justice, Duterte repeatedly said she did not trust the police, the courts or even the security personnel assigned to protect her.
“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” she told reporters and her lawyers.
Duterte said she had felt unsafe since 2023 due to the harassment of her family by certain authorities, whom she did not name.
She asked: “Who will answer for it if I die later tonight? Who will be held accountable?”
Duterte initially refused to enter the building, laying out several scenarios she feared could put her life at risk.
She worried that she could be placed in a small elevator with police officers, leaving her vulnerable.

She also pointed to firearms carried by the officers posted at the building and said she could no longer trust even her own security detail because, in her view, they were picked for the job by the Marcos administration.
The Vice President remained hesitant even when assured by her lawyers that they would stay by her side.
Standing near the staircase at the Hall of Justice, she recalled the 1983 assassination of former Sen. Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr.
“Do you remember that Ninoy Aquino died on the (airplane) staircase?” she asked her lawyers in Filipino.
Duterte then asked journalists to accompany her to the fifth floor, where she would post bail.
“I want a lot of people to see it. I really don’t know what will happen to me in there,” she said.
Her appeal effectively asked the media to serve as witnesses to whatever might happen to her inside the building.
The discussion between Duterte and her lawyers, held in front of reporters and police officers, went on for about 40 minutes before Poa finally persuaded her to go inside.
Duterte later said her lawyers advised her to post bail rather than be in police custody.

“They explained that I would be better protected by civilians who could see and notice my situation, compared to remaining in detention where I would be isolated and have less protection,” she said in a statement released by the Office of the Vice President.
Duterte also expressed concern for the safety of her mother and children.

Lim said Duterte’s lawyers were considering possible legal action over the implementation of the warrant, particularly after she alleged that authorities had gone to places where her mother and children were staying.
Duterte said government pressure and harassment against her family had continued since 2023.
Her allegations have not been independently verified, and Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Duterte had not reported any threats to the police.
“To date, however, the Vice President has not reported to the PNP any threat to her life or to the safety of her family, including the threats she said date back to 2023,” Nartatez said.
He added that the PNP had not monitored any incident posing danger to Duterte or her family.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said authorities “knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest.”
Remulla said the PNP had body-camera footage of the serving of the warrant and of Duterte’s arrival at the Hall of Justice.
Historic arrest, routine bail
“The PNP accorded her all the respect her position deserves,” he said, adding that the pressure surrounding Duterte’s situation appeared to be affecting her perception.
As the Vice President left the Hall of Justice after posting bail, her supporters gathered outside chanted “Duterte! Duterte!”
She hugged one of them, who was weeping, before proceeding to her vehicle.

Duterte’s lawyers stressed that she was not given special treatment. Lim said his client voluntarily appeared before the court that issued the warrant, so there was no need for her to be physically arrested and have her mug shot taken.
“She had to go through the same process,” Lim said.

As part of the process, the court received the photos provided by Duterte, an affidavit of undertaking, a barangay certification of her Davao City residence, a sketch of her Davao home and a government-issued ID.

But Lim explained that posting bail did not mean Duterte had already surrendered to the court’s jurisdiction. He said her legal team continued to assert that an impeachable officer like the Vice President could not be criminally charged while in office.
Constitutional law professor Paolo Emmanuel Tamase of the University of the Philippines College of Law disputed that view.
“There’s no basis in Philippine constitutional law for the immunity of a vice president from any type of suit, including a criminal suit,” Tamase said.
Unlike the president, who enjoys immunity from suit while in office, the vice president does not have the same constitutional protection, he said.
Tamase also distinguished impeachment from criminal liability.
Impeachment concerns the removal of an impeachable public official, he said, while a criminal case seeks to hold an official accountable for an alleged criminal act.
“If that argument were to be respected or to be given weight, you would have … at least 30 officers who are impeachable and therefore cannot be sued,” Tamase said.
Such an interpretation would create a major gap in the system for holding public officials accountable, he added.

Tamase called Duterte’s arrest proceedings historically significant because she is the highest-ranking sitting public official in Philippine history to have been subjected to criminal prosecution and arrest proceedings.
The bail process itself, however, was routine because the charges are bailable, he said.
Tamase said the criminal case before the RTC and Senate impeachment proceedings are separate, although the arrest warrant could influence public opinion.

It could reinforce the view that Duterte’s statements constituted criminal threats, he said, but could also strengthen among her supporters the narrative that government institutions were being weaponized against her.
Duterte’s request for media to accompany her inside the Hall of Justice came amid that broader dispute over public trust in the institutions handling her cases.

blocks.caption: FEELING UNSAFE Vice President Sara Duterte tells the media on Saturday she distrusts even her own security escorts and asks them to accompany her to the fifth floor of the Quezon City Hall of Justice, where she later posted bail on three counts of grave threats filed against her. —Grig C. Montegr…

blocks.text: Not the first
Duterte is not the first Philippine vice president to face criminal complaints while in office.
During the presidency of her father, Rodrigo Duterte, then Vice President Leni Robredo was among opposition figures charged in 2019 in connection with the “Ang Totoong Narcolist” videos.

Robredo faced complaints for sedition, inciting to sedition, libel, cyberlibel, estafa, harboring a criminal and obstruction of justice. The complaints were based largely on allegations by Peter Joemel Advincula, the self-described narrator of the videos known as “Bikoy.”
The PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group filed the complaints against Robredo and other opposition figures in July 2019.

The Department of Justice dismissed the complaints against Robredo in February 2020 for lack of evidence and probable cause, before the cases reached trial. —WITH REPORTS FROM GILLIAN VILLANUEVA, AND ISABELLE PECHAY

articles.title: Eminent Cebuano scholar, National Artist Resil Mojares; 83
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Resil Mojares, a man of letters who led a panel of scholars whose findings definitively settled the decadeslong dispute over the site of the first Holy Mass in the country,…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Resil Mojares, a man of letters who led a panel of scholars whose findings definitively settled the decadeslong dispute over the site of the first Holy Mass in the country, died on Saturday.

“We are heartbroken to share the passing of our beloved father, Resil Buagas Mojares. He had just celebrated his 83rd birthday yesterday, and we are grateful to have spent his final day honoring and celebrating his life,” his daughter, Leigh Go Mojares, announced on social media.

A historian, Mojares chaired the body convened by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) in 2018 to review varying accounts about the site of the “first Mass,” in the runup to the government-led commemoration of the 500th year of the “Victory at Mactan” in 2021, which forms part of the quincentennial of the first circumnavigation of the world by Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan and his crew.
Parallel to that occasion, the Catholic Church was also gearing for the celebration of the 500th year of Christianity in the country.
For the effort, Mojares worked with Dr. Danilo Gerona, Dr. Francis Navarro, Dr. Carlos Madrid Alvarez-Piner, Dr. Jose Victor Torres, and Jesuit priest Antonio Francisco de Castro.

In constituting what would later be known as the “Mojares panel,” the NHCP and the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines agreed that the review pertains to the first Easter Sunday Mass in the country, referring to the event on March 31, 1521.
From 2018 to 2019, Mojares led the panel in assessing the competing claims over the site of the Mass.
‘True titan of local history’

It submitted a report recommending that the NHCP sustain Limasawa as the historical site. The NHCP later formalized the decision through a board resolution in 2020, ending the latest chapter in the long-running controversy over whether the historic rite took place in Limasawa or in Butuan.
Mojares’ work on the issue added to a career devoted to documenting Philippine history, culture and identity, particularly through the lens of local and regional studies.
On Saturday, the NHCP paid tribute to Mojares as “a true titan of local history.”
The commission noted his pioneering work in Philippine local studies and also his service as founding director of the University of San Carlos Cebuano Studies Center in 1975.
He also contributed to the Cebu Town History Project, where he wrote the history of Cebu province.
In 2018, Mojares was conferred the Order of National Artist for Literature for his contributions to Philippine scholarly and literary development.

The National Commission for Culture and the Arts described him as a leading figure in the promotion of regional literature and history, noting that his work spanned fiction, essays, journalism, biography, literature, history and cultural studies.
Major works

Among his major works were “The War Against the Americans: Resistance and Collaboration in Cebu Province,” “House of Memory: Essays,” “The Man Who Would Be President: Serging Osmeña” and “Philippine Politics, and Brains of the Nation.”

According to historian Patricio Abinales, Mojares had “an impressive body of work and an amazing contribution to Philippine Studies.” Between 1969 and 2017, he had 124 titles to his name, 107 sole authored and coauthored works, and four sole-edited and five coedited books.
Six of his works won the National Book Award.
“Peerless. Massive in quantity and of high quality,” award-winning writer Danton Remoto said on social media of Mojares’ work.
Mojares earned a bachelor’s degree in English and master’s degree in literature from University of San Carlos in Cebu, and a doctorate in literature from the University of the Philippines Diliman.
He is survived by his children Kim Carmel, Mark Soren, Ressa Gail and Anna Leigh, along with five grandchildren. /cb

articles.title: DOJ-led workshop: Bullying victims need not suffer in silence
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Bullied children should not try to seek retribution from their tormentors by themselves but should seek the assistance of persons in authority or other responsible adults. This…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Bullied children should not try to seek retribution from their tormentors by themselves but should seek the assistance of persons in authority or other responsible adults.
This was underscored by Justice Undersecretary Ian Norman Dato in the recent Anti-Bullying Information Workshop at Bagong Tanyag Integrated School (BTIS) in Taguig City.

The workshop was organized after several shooting incidents in schools that resulted in deaths and injuries of students. Bullying and school violence are becoming very serious problems that the House of Representatives has passed a bill declaring September as National Bullying Awareness Month.
One suspect reportedly claimed his action was in retaliation for the bullying he was getting in school.

“Do not try to fight back [when bullied],” Dato said. “Trust in the process.” He assured his audience consisting primarily of Grades 7 and 9 students and their parents that both the Departments of Education and Justice had people and strategies to address the growing problem of bullying and school violence.
Proactive campaign
Schools have teachers, guidance counselors and other experts to assist victims while DOJ prosecutors help when the offense violates laws. Free legal assistance is also available.

Dato added that parents should actively participate in the campaign against bullying. They should be proactive, monitoring their children for signs of bullying, rather than re-active—acting only after serious harm had occurred.
BTIS principal Donnabel Balantac said parents had to know the signs of bullying and help their children deal with the problem.
The justice official stressed that, under the law, bullying committed within a two-kilometer radius of a school was still considered an offense that the school could and should act on.
Republic Act 10627, the Anti-Bullying Act, was signed into law in 2013.
Role of bystanders
Dato said bullying could be physical, psychological and/or emotional, verbal, cyber, social (ostracizing the victim) or gender-based.

Bullying was also not just a matter between the victim and the bully. It also involved bystanders who witnessed or had personal knowledge of the incident and upstander or those who would try to protect or support the bullied.
Balantac stressed that bullying should never be tolerated. Respect for one another, she added, was needed to create a safer environment for children.
“Hindi ka nag-iisa (You are not alone),” Dato reassured bullying victims. /cb

articles.title: LTFRB taking steps on NLEx traffic jam
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Saturday said it has directed its regional offices to coordinate with operators of expressways in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Saturday said it has directed its regional offices to coordinate with operators of expressways in disseminating timely reports on the status of roads, following the weekend gridlock at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) from Aug. 28 to 31.

Acting LTFRB Chair Greg Pua Jr. has also instructed regional offices to coordinate with local government units in identifying alternative routes from expressways during emergencies or other unexpected incidents.

Furthermore, the regional offices were ordered to strengthen coordination with transport and trucker companies to ensure the “widest dissemination of information to the public in cases of unexpected road emergencies.”

The directive covers LTFRB offices in the Ilocos region, where the Tarlac-Pangasinan-La Union Expressway is located, Central Luzon with Subic-Clark-Tarlac Expressway and NLEx, as well as Metro Manila and Calabarzon with the South-Luzon Expressway, Southern Tagalog Arterial Road Toll, Cavite-Laguna Expressway and Muntinlupa-Cavite Expressway.

In a statement, the agency said “The LTFRB approach is two-pronged: the first focuses on information dissemination especially to the transport companies and the commuters, and the second is identification of alternative routes for wors[t]-case scenarios.”
‘Wake-up call’
“No motorists and commuters would want to be stuck in traffic jams for hours and the two approaches are essential for both the transport companies and commuters to plan their travel ahead,” it added.

In a letter dated Aug. 31, the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) asked NLEx Corp., the operator of NLEx, to submit a detailed explanation regarding the flooding incident that occurred in the expressway’s main carriageway, particularly in Tulaoc Bridge at San Simon, Pampanga, and the resulting heavy traffic.
Several netizens posted their experience driving for hours on social media, with one motorist saying her trip took 22 hours after she was forced to take detours.
Pua said the LTFRB aims to assist motorists in finding alternative routes should there be “unexpected incidents” in expressways.

“Our priority has always been the welfare of passengers and the delivery of goods to the Filipino people. The incident that happened in NLEx is a wake-up call for us in the LTFRB and other agencies to do our part in coming up with measures to maximize the assistance to the public,” he said. /cb

articles.title: Ombudsman: Still no SC action on complaint vs CA justices
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — After being advised to charge erring members of the judiciary, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday reminded the Supreme Court to act on a pending administrative…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — After being advised to charge erring members of the judiciary, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday reminded the Supreme Court to act on a pending administrative complaint against seven justices of the Court of Appeals (CA).
Remulla said his predecessor Samuel Martires filed in March last year a case of gross ignorance of law and conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service against these justices.

The complaint involves CA’s reversal of the preventive suspension orders issued by the Office of the Ombudsman against Antique officials, including Mayor Ernesto Tanjanlangit III of Tobias Fornier town.

The CA associate justices named in the complaint were Louis Acosta, Rex Bernando Pascual, Mary Charlene Hernandez-Azura, Roberto Quiroz, Ferdinand Baylon, Marlene Gonzales-Sison and Rafael Santos. Sison and Santos have since retired.
In his radio show “Executive Session,” Remulla said “To date, there appears no public record of the Judicial Integrity [Office] or the Supreme Court having acted or resolved that complaint.”
Antique case

The Ombudsman was also responding to a statement last week by SC spokesperson Camille Ting urging him to file charges against members of the judiciary if he has evidence of wrongdoing, since the high court could not act on broad accusations.

Remulla said the complaint pending with the Judicial Integrity Office, the SC’s investigating body on disciplinary cases in the judiciary, stemmed from the CA’s nullification of the Ombudsman’s preventive suspension order in 2024 against Tanjanlangit over a dispute with then Vice Mayor Jose Maria Fornier regarding a food pack distribution.

Remulla said these were just among the cases being “overruled” by the CA. “It’s about time that we examine the justice system … We cannot make the Supreme Court, (lower) courts, the judges and the justices of the appellate court sacred cows. There should be no sacred cows anymore,” he said. /cb

articles.title: US Open: Alex Eala looks for more improvement as she faces Iva Jovic
articles.summary: Alex Eala at the 2026 US Open: Schedule, draw and history Alex Eala is at the point in her career where the process matters as much as the results. The 21-year-old star has often said she doesn’t set…

blocks.text: Alex Eala plans to serve up a strong performance against Iva Jovic. Her fans are hoping that results in a win. —KEATS LONDON
Alex Eala at the 2026 US Open: Schedule, draw and history
Alex Eala is at the point in her career where the process matters as much as the results.
The 21-year-old star has often said she doesn’t set hard year-end targets at this point, preferring to measure how she has improved from tournament to tournament.
That is how she views her latest US Open stint.

“I think experience is definitely helpful,” she told reporters after her second-round 6-1, 6-4 victory over Oleksandra Oliynykova of Ukraine. “I do feel like [I’m] a more well-rounded player now and more mature. I guess with time comes maturity and [becoming] more intelligent.”
“I think I just have more knowledge with the experience in terms of tennis and competing at the very high level and knowledge of what I’m capable of and much more belief in myself.”

But the large Filipino community in Queens, New York, that lives near the US Open venue in Flushing Meadows will certainly be counting results, as they keep shelling out big bucks to catch Eala in the flesh—even if she is just doing practice sets.

Eala is scheduled to battle Iva Jovic next, a third-round match whose exact first serve is yet to be determined at press time. Eala and Jovic are close friends and are part of a close-knit group of young rising stars on the WTA Tour. The more pressing piece of trivia to tennis fans, however, is that the 18-year-old Jovic is 2-0 against Eala so far.

“Yeah, I’m super excited [to face Eala],” Jovic said after her 6-4, 6-4 win over Briton Francesca Jones in Thursday’s second round. “The atmosphere is gonna be amazing, and she’s been playing some great tennis.”

Eala said she has learned to manage her emotions and mental approach to games that involve her close friends. What she is focusing more on is the fact that some of her friends pose a stern test as she bids to make a deep run at the US Open.

“I’ve encountered my fair share of challenges against her this year,” the world No. 17 said. “But yeah, I mean it’s not under my control who I play, and all I can do is, you know, give my best and try to do everything that I can to win.”

Jovic is looking to surpass her best career Grand Slam showing—a quarterfinal run at the Australian Open this year. She shot to prominence with her maiden WTA title at Guadalajara last year at the age of 17 and arrived at Flushing Meadows at a career-high ranking of 14 in the world.

Eala, on the other hand, has been on a tear the last couple of months. She beat defending champion Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon and went through a very tough draw to win her first WTA title in Washington. Both of Jovic’s victories over Eala came before that breakthrough title—in the first round at Roland Garros this year and in the round of 16 at Queen’s Club in London.
“She’s an amazing player,” Eala said of Jovic. “Young, very talented and very intelligent, of course. She’s a high-ranked player and very, very accomplished.”

Whatever happens in that match, trust that Eala will be looking more at how she played than on the eventual result. But for the Filipino community that has waited a year to see her back, a positive result would even be more meaningful. —WITH A REPORT FROM AFP

articles.title: Inquirer business reporter wins PIDS media award
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Inquirer business reporter Ian Nicolas P. Cigaral of the Philippine Daily Inquirer has been recognized by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) for his work in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Inquirer business reporter Ian Nicolas P. Cigaral of the Philippine Daily Inquirer has been recognized by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) for his work in bringing research-based economic and development issues to a wider audience.

Cigaral received the “Kwentista ng Pananaliksik: Most Supportive Print/Online Journalist” award at this year’s Saliksik at Balita: PIDS Media Awards, which honors journalists who help translate policy research into public understanding.
PIDS, the government’s primary socioeconomic policy research institution, cited Cigaral for his “outstanding contributions to research-informed public discourse.”
Macroeconomy, banking

Cigaral received the award Tuesday in Quezon City from PIDS president Philip Arnold Tuaño, former Presidential Communications Operations Office Secretary Herminio Coloma Jr. and PIDS vice president Marife Ballesteros.

Cigaral has covered a range of economic and financial issues during his years at the Inquirer. He began by reporting on public finance and the broader macroeconomy before moving to the central bank and banking beats.

The award was presented during the kickoff forum and press conference for the 24th Development Policy Research Month, an annual observance held every September under Proclamation No. 247, issued in 2002.
The monthlong event seeks to highlight the role of policy research in national development and encourage public discussion of issues affecting the country.

This year’s theme, “Building Strong Institutions, Unlocking Human Capital Potential,” focuses on the role of effective, accountable, and resilient institutions in turning investments in education, health, labor markets, and social protection into greater economic opportunity and a better quality of life. /cb

articles.title: It’s next matchup for Creamline after first loss
articles.summary: Jaja Santiago-Minowa and the Creamline Cool Smashers are taking their first loss of the PVL Invitational Conference in stride, and will shift their attention to trying to book a ticket to the finals…

blocks.text: Jaja Santiago-Minowa and the Cool Smashers will gun for a title berth against PLDT. —PVL IMAGES

Jaja Santiago-Minowa and the Creamline Cool Smashers are taking their first loss of the PVL Invitational Conference in stride, and will shift their attention to trying to book a ticket to the finals when they battle defending champion PLDT on Sunday.

Santiago-Minowa and the Cool Smashers saw their three-game unbeaten run ended by a quick and gritty EST Cola side, 17-25, 25-21, 25-22, 27-25, as the Thais forced a tie at 3-1 at the top of the standings on Friday night at Smart Araneta Coliseum.

“I think our problem today was our out-of-system blocking. We had the passing and the attack, but we struggled with our out-of-system block. They scored a lot against us in those situations, especially their lefty,” said Santiago-Minowa in Filipino after her 19-point effort wasn’t enough.

“I think that’s also something we need to work on before facing PLDT. We have to work twice as hard because we only have two games left. We need to bounce back quickly since we only have one day to prepare, and our next game is on Sunday.”
Creamline, which settled for bronze in last year’s weeklong tournament, tries to complete its comeback to the Invitational final against the defending champion PLDT at 6:30 p.m.
“I think it’s about taking it one point at a time and one set at a time. Everyone is preparing and everyone wants to win,” said Santiago-Minowa.

“It’s about how you overcome the pressure, how you step up and play harder, and how much you want the win. Everyone is already tired, so at this point, it’s really about who can endure until the end.”

Four teams are still fighting for the two finals slots, with Creamline and EST Cola tied at 3-1. Nxled and PLDT are knotted at 2-2, with the reigning champs holding a 7-6 edge in the FIVB point-system tiebreak.
Creamline and EST Cola, which takes on Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City at 4 p.m., need to win both of their matches to set a winner-take-all game on Tuesday.

Papatchaya Phontham erupted for 27 points off 24 kills, two blocks and an ace to beat Creamline. Nannaphat Moonjakham had 16 points and 15 excellent receptions. Nirarach Srikuta tallied 12 points and 15 receptions, while setter Serah Ankomah, who also translates for the team in interviews, was a revelation from the bench with 13 excellent sets.

Santiago-Minowa already met some of the members of EST Cola, who won three straight games in the PVL. The Thais held a training camp when the Filipino middle blocker was still with Osaka Marvelous in the Japan SV.League.

“They’re really impressive. I actually know some of them because I think they’re the next generation. They had a training camp in Japan with Osaka Marvelous, the team I played for two years ago,” said Santiago-Minowa.

“They’re under 18, and their improvement has been incredible. Their outside hitters and opposite are really powerful. It’s impressive to see players that young playing at that level. We really have to find a way to overcome that.”

The Chameleons need to win their final elimination game against the Farm Fresh Foxies in three or four sets at 1:30 p.m. and hope for either Creamline or EST Cola to lose to make it to the championship match.
Savi Davison and the High Speed Hitters need a loss from Nxled in the first game and to pull off a big win over the 11-time champion to keep their title defense going. INQ

articles.title: Returning Carlos Alcaraz vows to take more breaks
articles.summary: NEW YORK—Feeling better than he expected after a four-month absence, Carlos Alcaraz is planning to take more breaks during the tennis season. Alcaraz returned to play at the US Open after being…

blocks.text: Carlos Alcaraz of Spain reacts with partner Serena Williams of the United States in their mixed doubles match against Erin Routliffe of New Zealand and Lloyd Glasspool of the United Kingdom during Fan Week at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 25, 2026 in the Flushing neighborhood of the Queens borough of New York City. Sarah Stier/Getty Images/AFP
NEW YORK—Feeling better than he expected after a four-month absence, Carlos Alcaraz is planning to take more breaks during the tennis season.

Alcaraz returned to play at the US Open after being sidelined since April by a right wrist injury. The defending champion advanced to the fourth round Friday with a 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 victory over Wu Yibing.
He said his body feels good and he’s had no setbacks after his matches.

“It feels like I’ve been competing the whole time. So I surprise myself the way that I’m feeling and the way that I’m recovering after every match,” Alcaraz said. “So I’m just really happy about it that I’m able to perform at my best after every match.”

Alcaraz said the injury that forced him to withdraw during the Barcelona Open wasn’t caused by playing too much, so taking time off next year wouldn’t be for physical reasons. Rather, he believes it would provide him a mental benefit.
“I’m kind of a guy that doesn’t need to play a lot of tournaments,” Alcaraz said, explaining he preferred to be “mentally healthy.”
“I just feel like you can have those moments of time to have a break,” he added, “to prepare well for tournaments, to prepare well mentally.”
He debuted a new look Friday, with a white shirt underneath his sleeveless shirt, and has a new celebration, mimicking shooting an arrow.
The wardrobe change was apparently because just one shirt was moving around too much in the previous match.
“I think I saw my nipple too much lately,” he said. “I felt like, you know, I could hide it for at least one match.”
The celebration choice came from his brothers.
“They made me choose to do the arrow or dancing, so I didn’t have any doubts about choosing the arrow,” Alcaraz said. “So I will ask them what’s next if I win the next round.”

Alcaraz played 80 matches last year and was 22-3, including his seventh major championship at the Australian Open, when he was hurt this year. Like many players, he is worried about the length of the tennis season and the number of tournaments.
Unlike many of them, he doesn’t have serious ranking or financial concerns if he chooses to skip some events.

“It is like it’s tournament after tournament after tournament, and you don’t feel like you are well-prepared coming to some tournaments,” Alcaraz said. “So that’s why I just decided that probably in the future I’m going to take breaks because I want to feel well prepared coming to Grand Slams, Masters 1000s, whatever it is.”
Sitting out for longer periods would surely help the 23-year-old physically, and Alcaraz ultimately thinks it will make him happier. —AP

articles.title: Sketching Cagayan de Oro’s vanishing heritage
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY, Philippines — Like-minded residents in this “City of Golden Friendship” have banded together to preserve the locality’s past grandeur and charming heritage before they are lost…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY, Philippines — Like-minded residents in this “City of Golden Friendship” have banded together to preserve the locality’s past grandeur and charming heritage before they are lost to time.
There are no strict rules, gallery dress codes, entry fees, age or gender restrictions, and no fancy or expensive gadgets required.
What they have are sketchbooks balanced on their knees, pens and ink, folding wooden stools set up on dusty sidewalks, and a shared, quiet urgency to capture a city gradually slipping through time.
When the Carmen Art District issued an open call for an informal urban sketching gathering downtown, it unlocked an unexpected groundswell of interest.

Architecture students from the University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines (USTP) sat alongside 12-year-old novices, seasoned visual artists and corporate workers eager to trade glowing computer screens for paper and graphite.

On Aug. 2, this diverse gathering lined the busy junction of Capistrano and Cruz Taal streets, sketch pads, pencils and ink bottles in hand, transforming an old downtown cinema and its surrounding heritage structures into a living, open-air studio.

The initiative grew organically from informal conversations among local creatives searching for tangible ways to document Cagayan de Oro’s historic edifices before modern redevelopment sweeps them away.

Artist Kathz Gaid, a member of Urban Sketchers Manila, brought the idea to fellow co-founders Kelly Ramos and Nathalie Mariano: scout a heritage location, drop a pin online and let the public assemble on the curb.

blocks.caption: PRESERVING MEMORIES Armed with sketch pads and pencils, local artists and young participants gather downtown to document Cagayan de Oro’s vanishing heritage, capturing historic landmarks and the city’s architectural character before modern redevelopment erases their traces.

blocks.text: Casual setup
“In the third session, that was when we opened it to the public,” Ramos, owner and art director of Carmen Art District, told the Inquirer.

“We told everyone there were no requirements, no fees — just bring a pen or pencil and sketch with us. People really just started coming. We were surprised by how many were already sitting alongside us,” Ramos added.

The casual setup quickly fostered spontaneous community connections that traditional studio spaces rarely provide. During a gathering outside the historic Velez House along the boulevard, the homeowner came outside and chatted with the artists on the pavement, sharing the building’s origins and architectural quirks.

blocks.caption: What they have are sketchbooks balanced on their knees, pens and ink, folding wooden stools set up on dusty sidewalks, and a shared, quiet urgency to capture a city gradually slipping through time.

blocks.text: That documentation later took on a poignant, tragic weight when the Velez heritage house was razed by fire after the sketchers had gathered there and drawn its wooden architecture.
“At least we accidentally immortalized the Velez house with that sketch session before it was gone,” Ramos told the Inquirer.

Operating out of an ancestral home in the Carmen district, the art collective views these old edifices not merely as nostalgic drawing subjects but as vital cultural touchstones standing precariously at the crossroads of commercial growth.

For Ramos, who served as a curator for five years at the La Castilla Museum in Liceo de Cagayan University, urban sketching offers a hands-on, democratic way to rescue forgotten or neglected heritage sites from obscurity while stimulating local tourism and civic awareness.

blocks.caption: Capturing historic landmarks and the city’s architectural character before modern redevelopment erases their traces.

blocks.text: ‘Irreplaceable’

“These old houses are either abandoned or sitting unused, yet they remain irreplaceable cultural treasures we ought to appreciate,” Ramos said. “Urban sketching promotes that appreciation. It becomes an immediate jumping point for discussions on the layered history of Cagayan de Oro.”
The movement has also earned support from veteran cultural advocates.

Nicolas Aca, resident artist and gallery curator of Capitol University’s Museum of Three Cultures and chairman of the City Historical Commission, joined a recent gathering to show his support and champion the grassroots effort to document old and historic structures through sketching.

“For now, we encourage artists to sketch historical sites and old structures of the city. A lot of artists participated, asked questions, and were really engaged. In the future, we are considering an exhibition of these outputs for educational purposes,” he told the Inquirer.

blocks.caption: ARTFUL STROKES Local artists put their sketches to paper

blocks.text: To maintain the initiative’s open spirit, organizers deliberately avoid formal hierarchies, membership rosters or centralized group chats under the Carmen Art District.

“We want it to be as inclusive and informal as possible so that anyone can join without any barriers or gatekeeping,” Ramos said. “If participants want to make their own group chats within their networks, they can, but our goal is simply to hold a regular session and that’s it.”
On Aug. 16, the group held another sketching session at the Montalvan ancestral house on Burgos Street, followed by a sketch walk toward Gaston Park, where seasonal plants were on display.
The artists returned to the streets on Aug. 28, as the city celebrated its annual patronal fiesta, the Higalaay Festival.

This time, they sketched the distinctive yellow-and-red, two-story wooden heritage house at the corner of Velez and Hayes streets, preserving another irreplaceable fragment of Kagay-anon memory from oblivion, one stroke at a time. /cb

articles.title: South Korea exposes urgent Gilas needs for title defense
articles.summary: Coach Tim Cone acknowledged there was plenty left to be desired after Gilas Pilipinas got beaten badly by South Korea on Friday in the first of two tuneup games between the two teams before the…

blocks.text: Justine Baltazar: Bright spot —FIBA PHOTO

Coach Tim Cone acknowledged there was plenty left to be desired after Gilas Pilipinas got beaten badly by South Korea on Friday in the first of two tuneup games between the two teams before the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
But Cone would rather see his 11-man crew play badly at this point than during the Asiad, where Gilas will look to defend its gold.
“We weren’t good, no doubt,” Cone said a day after Gilas’ 81-55 in Suwon, South Korea, where the exhibition series is being held.
“But we don’t need to be good right now. We need to be good a week from now when the Asian Games starts,” he added.

It wasn’t the first time this version of Gilas got some hardcourt action, having split a pair of scrimmages with the team that, last weekend, swept the fourth window of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers.
But the series is the first look at how the all-PBA squad measures against a continental rival.

And right from the opening tip, Gilas found some immediate needs to work on, trailing 9-0 at the start, then failing to gain more ground after cutting the deficit to 21-18 late in the first quarter. The team spent the rest of the game playing catch-up and eventually falling by a huge margin
Shooting was something that was an eyesore, as the Filipinos went 23-of-82 from the field for a 28-percent clip, while its defense had no answer for South Korea’s outside shots.
Lee Hyung-jun led the way for South Korea with 27 points on seven triples, on top of three rebounds, five assists and two steals.

Justine Baltazar was among the few bright spots with 15 points, 10 rebounds, two assists and three steals, while Adrian Nocum scored 10. The gutsy Rian or Sine guard, however, shot 4-of-13 from the field.

Robert Bolick dished out five assists and grabbed four rebounds but was 1-of-8 for only two points in 26 minutes. His exposure in the match is a likely prelude to how he’ll be used during the Asian Games.
Gilas and South Korea will meet again on Sunday afternoon to conclude the series, before the two squads head to Japan for the Asiad. Cone would like to see the rematch serve some purpose.
“We’ll use this and Sunday’s game to get better,” Cone said. “Guys are still feeling each other out, learning to play together, learning what their roles are.”
“I believe we’ll settle in and figure it out. This team is really motivated,” he added. INQ

articles.title: Restore funding for Edsa busway
articles.summary: The Edsa busway is one of the casualties of the cuts made to the Department of Transportation’s (DOTr) proposed budget for next year—getting zero allocation. The busway, also known as the Edsa…

blocks.text: The Edsa busway is one of the casualties of the cuts made to the Department of Transportation’s (DOTr) proposed budget for next year—getting zero allocation.

The busway, also known as the Edsa carousel, operates on a dedicated inner median bus lane along Edsa. It carries a daily ridership of more than 180,000 and has served 341 million passengers since it opened in June 2020.

This only shows how crucial the 28-kilometer busway has become in moving commuters in Metro Manila, notorious for its traffic gridlock. The DOTr stated last year that the busway “continues to be one of the most efficient public road transport systems” in the metro. Per the agency’s data, it reached a single-day peak of 321,186 passengers in April 2025 and posted 6.53 million ridership alone in December last year during the busy holiday season.

The busway currently has 23 northbound stops and 24 southbound stops connecting Monumento in the north to Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) in the south. The busway stops include the one in Kamuning, whose renovation cost P87.3 million, along with the replacement of the infamous steep footbridge nearby—known as Mount Kamuning—with a modernized overpass. President Marcos even led the inspection of the new station last March and praised the undertaking, noting that improvements like this can be done after all.
Commuting experience

“It’s not that difficult, as long as we are determined to improve the commuting experience,” he said. “Commuting is already difficult, considering the long lines and the heat … We should really address what our fellow citizens go through every day just to get to work and get back home.”

The President vowed to address the infrastructure problems, including the proper maintenance of new facilities. But those words now sound hollow with his administration’s decision to defund the Edsa busway.

Last May, DOTr sought an increase in the busway’s budget to P1.32 billion from this year’s P88.71 million to sustain its expansion and maintenance and support the process of unifying the design and engineering of each station.

The DOTr already started last year the P247.59-million rehabilitation of the Monumento, Bagong Barrio, North Avenue, and Guadalupe busway stations. It also recently issued a P264.86-million contract to develop new stations located in Cubao, Magallanes, and PITX.
12 more busway stations

Its budget for next year would have been used to rehabilitate the remaining stations amid a projected increase in the busway’s passenger traffic. According to the DOTr, annual ridership went up by 5.89 percent to 66.67 million last year from 63.02 million in 2024. The agency is projecting the number to increase to 70 million passengers this year.

At the DOTr’s budget hearing this week, Senior Undersecretary Mark Steven Pastor said the maintenance and operations of the busway system could suffer from the budget cut. This would compromise the security of passengers, as the salaries and contracts of the Special Action and Intelligence Committee for Transportation and security services are under the project management office. Rehabilitation of 12 more busway stations next year, estimated to cost P1.7 billion, will also be affected.

The Move As One Coalition said the zero funding was not consistent with the Marcos administration’s transport goals and the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028. “A supermajority—94 percent—of Filipinos do not own cars … Why are their mobility needs not reflected in the proposed National Expenditure Program 2027?” the coalition said in a statement.
A significant milestone

Several lawmakers have also called for the restoration of the busway’s budget, with Akbayan party list Rep. Percival Cendaña saying that “The thousands of commuters who rely on public transportation must be prioritized.”

The government planned to privatize the busway by end of last year. But based on statements from the DOTr as of May this year, the decision on whether to privatize was still pending, and no proposals have been put forward so far. The government also intended to complete the rehabilitation of the stations before turning operations over to a private firm. So why abandon a vital service and leave it without funding at this time? This is tantamount to abandoning the hundreds of thousands of commuters who rely on the busway and is a reflection of the government’s utter disregard for their welfare.

While the Marcos administration’s ambitious P197.3 billion budget for the country’s rail transport program in 2027 is a significant milestone, a railway cannot serve the needs of commuters alone and must be complemented by other modes of transport. This means that the government must also invest in road public transit such as the Edsa busway to provide commuters with more options in a truly integrated transit network. Otherwise, the country’s transport system will remain broken and fragmented—and a daily nightmare for commuters—the way it is today.

articles.title: Living with water
articles.summary: The Kansai International Airport (KIX) in Japan opened in 1994 on an artificial island in Osaka Bay; it now sits on two. The seabed there lies 18 meters down, under rock and soil dumped from three…

blocks.text: The Kansai International Airport (KIX) in Japan opened in 1994 on an artificial island in Osaka Bay; it now sits on two. The seabed there lies 18 meters down, under rock and soil dumped from three nearby mountains, over a soft layer of Holocene clay that was drained through millions of sand drains. Under the weight of the landfill and the structures above it, the first island has settled by 13 meters. Yet it remains a busy airport, operating 24 hours and serving about 30 million passengers a year.

The engineers expected the ground to sink. What they got wrong was by how much and how fast. Their forecasts covered the clay they had drained; the surprise came from Pleistocene layers hundreds of meters below. By 1990, before the airport opened, the island had settled well beyond prediction. To compensate for the subsidence that continues to this day, the engineers secured the airport with gigantic columns and jacks that can lift entire sections of the terminal.

They missed out badly only once, in September 2018, when Typhoon “Jebi” drove unusually high storm surges across Osaka Bay. Waves overtopped the seawall and flooded a runway and the terminal basements. An unmoored tanker was blown into the bridge linking the airport to the mainland. Full operations resumed in two weeks. With the airport running, 6 kilometers of the surrounding seawall was raised over three years. It was the second time this happened. The wall was first raised after a 2004 flooding. But Jebi exceeded it. Still, the Japanese engineers did not treat the water as insurmountable. They built a system for it and corrected the system when it failed.

The recent floods in Metro Manila, Bulacan, and Pampanga revived the question whether we can ever control flooding in the places on which the core of our metropolis stands. Perhaps this is the wrong question. The better one might be: what would it take to keep urban life viable where recurrent flooding is a fact of life?

The comparison with Kansai is instructive precisely because an airport is not a city. KIX is a single organization, with one operator, and a crew of engineers who have been taking yearly readings of the subsidence at fixed points since 1987. A metropolis has no such body. What looks like ingenuity in the Japanese case is an arrangement in which measuring, remembering, and correcting are somebody’s designated job.

For better or worse, our ancestors built beside the sea and the rivers, as one would in an archipelago. Our towns and cities grew on ground made unstable by monsoon rains, typhoons, storm surges, and the swelling of rivers from the mountains. They learned to adapt. What changed was the scale: farmland and marsh converted into subdivisions, groundwater pumped until the coastal towns began sinking faster than the sea was rising, and an engineering system that promised finality instead of regular maintenance

Flood control, in short, is not merely an engineering problem but a governance problem that presumes institutional memory, continuous monitoring, and a reliable system of warnings. The engineering is the manageable part; solutions tried elsewhere are available. What is lacking is the memory. We remember the disasters and their magnitude, far less the adjustments that followed, and almost nothing about whether they worked.

The reason is not a character flaw. In a functionally differentiated society, as Niklas Luhmann argued, there is no single entity in which such a memory could be stored. Each sector retains only what its own code can process. Politics remembers the culprits, because we keep an exact record of who stole the flood control money, even as we set this aside at election time. Media remembers events, because news requires novelty and faces. Science remembers the hydrology, but its warnings do not bind anyone. No one asks how well the Manggahan Floodway performed, and what we changed afterward? Its designers go uncredited; such projects draw attention only when they fail.

This is why a flood changes nothing even though it is everywhere at once. Luhmann wrote that a system genuinely resonates when it actually reorganizes its operations in response to environmental events. It does not merely talk about the environment while operating as before. Much of what we do after a catastrophic flood is to express irritation, assign blame, or write bills in the futile hope that ecological problems can be solved by law.

Then, there is the paradox that surfaces wherever protection succeeds: as when an effective solution to flooding invites continued settlement of the very areas it protects, by informal settlers with nowhere else to go and by developers who carve housing projects out of low-lying farmland. Every solution creates the conditions of the next problem.
The engineers at Kansai Airport did not stop the sinking. Instead, they provided for a system of continuous adjustment. That is the part we have not copied.
public.lives@gmail.com

articles.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
articles.summary:
Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffick drugs

An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for…

blocks.text: An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

articles.title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flood disaster
articles.summary:
Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate…

blocks.text: Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations on Saturday, as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.
Experts have said that as time passes, the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.
Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.
At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

articles.title: How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country?
articles.summary: The US mother was on trial for strangling her three children. In other western countries, there’s a specific law for mums who kill their young children.

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to unanimously decide on a verdict. The US mother was on trial for strangling her three children.

In a number of other western countries, there's a specific law on the books to deal with mothers who kill their young children. It's a term known as infanticide – and generally applies to the killing of a baby in the first year of their life.
Co-host of the BBC's Global Story podcast Asma Khalid explains how Lindsay Clancy's case might have unfolded differently elsewhere.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK
articles.summary:
US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after disaster
articles.summary:
Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped in depth of 170 metres

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.

The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst-affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods, according to army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.

Sanjay Shah was the first to be rescued and was taken to the Nepal army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, was also rescued from the tunnel. They were rescued from a depth of 170 metres inside the tunnel, confirmed Basnet.
Sanjay Shah was foreman at Upper Trishuli 3A and Kabir Maharjan was a superviser.
Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”
Describing his ordeal, Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood.

“Usually there would be only five or six people there but at this time there must have been around 40 to 45 people inside,” he said. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives. After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.
“While trying to get everyone out, I told them that there had been a major accident at the dam and urged everyone to run. In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself.”
To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had been communicating with only three or four others.
“They were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.
Officials said the two men were in stable condition and flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Nepal’s communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,”he wrote on social media.

Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

blocks.caption: A survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters

blocks.text: At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.

Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try and clear debris from the tunnel entrance. It was confirmed that voices of many people had been heard inside after a breakthrough was made on early Friday morning.
After the rescue team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you,” they received a response from inside: “OK.”

At least 557 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

Families of those missing in the tunnels have been gathering at hospitals in Kathmandu and at the Nepal electricity office for nine days, desperate for answers about their relatives. Posters of workers missing in Trishuli 3A and other projects line the wall of Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital.
In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.
